Rdio Scanner

Administrator Guide

Version 8.0.0. 1 · What Rdio Scanner is, and what this guide covers

Rdio Scanner ingests the audio files a software-defined radio recorder writes, files them against the system, site, talkgroup, and unit they came from, and serves them to listeners as a scanner. This guide is about the server: the program you install, the flags and options that configure it, the administration interface you use to set it up, and the APIs it answers on.

A deployment is one program. It listens on one address, keeps one database, and offers two interfaces: the main interface that listeners open, and the administration interface at /admin/ that you configure the deployment with. Everything in this guide is about the server and the administration interface.

How the name is said

Rdio Scanner /ˈreɪ.di.oʊ ˈskæn.ər/ RAY-dee-oh SCAN-er

What's new since version 6.6.3

Version 7 was assembled and never published, so an administrator coming from version 6.6.3 sees version 7 and version 8 at once. This is the short list of what changed since that release, with the chapter that operates it. The project's change log is the full history, release by release; what is here is what changes your work.

The changes since version 6.6.3, by what they touch
AreaWhat changedChapter
The logEvery entry names the part of the server that wrote it, and the log view filters on it. Messages no longer begin with the name of the internal function that wrote them. The view gained a subsystem filter, a text search, the clickable counts strip, and auto-refresh. Retention says what it removed, and says when it could not run. Lines that only ever went to the console are in the log now.14
The databaseA new schema, and four dialects: SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. The first start on a version 6.6.3 database migrates it in place, announces each table, and copies what it cannot carry into the migration archive instead of throwing it away.7, 24
The administration interfaceRebuilt. Sections are edited as a working copy and written with the save bar; the conflict banner appears when another session saved the same section; the systems-and-talkgroups dialog scopes a credential; the OpenAPI section reads the contract the server publishes; the Tools section exports and imports the configuration, and imports a talkgroup or unit list per system.8, 15
Talkgroups, groups, and tagsA talkgroup belongs to many groups, which is why the tag toggle is gone. System and talkgroup types name the radio standard, and the AFS systems option is gone, replaced by the Provoice type. Alert tones and LED colours are set at group, tag, system, and talkgroup level, with the group winning. Calls are delayed per system and per talkgroup.11, 12
Duplicate detectionDetection is built on the new schema, and the window is fixed: two calls on the same system, talkgroup, and site within half a second are one call.13
Getting audio inThe mask gained the unit label token, so a recorder that names the radio that transmitted names the unit the listener sees.10
Interfaces and APIsThe API was renewed with the older calls clients use kept working. The call history endpoints accept a listener's access code beside an administrator's session. The Model Context Protocol endpoint lets an assistant read a deployment, and write to it when it presents the administrator's credential.16, 17
The releaseThe archive carries this guide as its operating documentation, with the ffmpeg licence as plain text beside the program.4

Back up the configuration and the database before updating. The migration rewrites the database in place and removes an old table only once every row in it has been carried or archived, and every open administrator session ends on the first start of the new server. Chapter 24 is the path, start to finish.

What this guide does not cover

The scanner webapp — the application a listener opens on the main address, with its talkgroup list, its call history, its player, and its live feed — is not covered here. It is a separate application with its own guide, the scanner webapp's guide kept beside this one in the project's documentation. The native mobile applications are Saubeo Solutions' own clients, and they are not covered either. No screenshot in this guide shows a scanner webapp screen. Where a chapter needs to say something about what a listener sees, it says it from the server's side: the option that changes it, the credential that unlocks it, the endpoint that serves it.

One document, no loose ends

This guide is the path from nothing to a working deployment, and it is written to be read in order once and consulted afterwards. It is complete on its own terms: the operating detail for Linux, Windows, macOS, and FreeBSD is in chapter 21; the container image, its volume, and its user are in chapter 4; the log's subsystems and what each one reports are in chapter 14; the licence and the API access position are in chapter 27. Nothing in this guide asks you to open another file: every cross-reference is a chapter of this guide.

Reading this guide offline

This file carries its own stylesheet and its own pictures. It opens from an extracted release archive, a mail attachment, or a USB stick with no network, and it prints with a page break at each chapter. It links to nothing outside itself, so there is nothing to fail to load.

2 · How audio flows through the server

Audio arrives in one of two ways, is filed against the configuration, and leaves toward listeners. Understanding the path explains most of what you will configure, and most of what can go wrong.

In

A recorder's output reaches the server by one of these paths:

  • Dirwatch — the server watches a directory the recorder writes into, reads each new audio file, and takes the call's identity from the file's name, its MP3 tags, or its sidecar JSON, depending on the recorder type you chose for that watch. See Getting audio in.
  • The upload endpoints — a recorder posts the audio and its metadata to POST /api/call-upload, the endpoint that takes the call's fields as form fields, or posts trunk-recorder's JSON sidecar to POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-upload, the older endpoint that reads the sidecar as a document, marked deprecated in chapter 10 and on its way out. Both present an API key. See The HTTP REST API.

Both paths end at the same ingest. The ingest resolves the system, site, talkgroup, and unit the metadata names against your configuration. When Auto populate is on, an identity the configuration does not know is created on the spot; when it is off, the call is refused and the log says why. The ingest then converts the audio to AAC in an m4a container when the Audio conversion option asks for it, which is what makes recordings small and playable in a browser, and files the call in the database with its audio.

Audio lives in the database

The server stores the recordings inside the database, not as files beside it. The directory the server serves holds the database, the configuration file, and the server's own state — the recordings are rows. That is what makes a single file the whole archive of a deployment, and it is what you back up.

Out

  • Listeners read the call history and the recordings over the HTTP REST API, and follow live calls over the server's real-time channel. The REST API is free to use for any purpose; the real-time channel is proprietary, reserved for Saubeo Solutions and its native applications, as chapter 27 states.
  • Downstreams forward calls to another Rdio Scanner deployment, presenting an API key there, scoped to the systems and talkgroups you choose.

What the server keeps

What the server holds, and where
ThingWhere it livesChanged by
Systems, sites, talkgroups, units, groups, tags, access codes, API keys, dirwatches, downstreams, optionsThe database, edited as sections in the administration interfaceYou, in a section, saved with that section's save bar
Recorded calls and their audioThe databaseThe ingest, when audio arrives
The logThe database, read in the Logs sectionThe server, as it works
Flags: addresses, database connection, TLS, servicerdio-scanner.ini in the base directory, written by -config_saveYou, in the file, or on the command line

The split matters at configuration time: the sections are saved through the running server and are announced to every open administration session, while the flags are read at start-up and need a restart.

3 · Requirements

The server is one program with a database behind it. What you need is a machine that runs one of the released platforms, a place to keep the data, and a recorder whose output the server can read.

Platforms a release is built for

The release matrix, as the build tool defines it. Every release carries its own ffmpeg inside the program; the macOS and FreeBSD ffmpeg binaries are compiled on the platform each target runs on, and the build adopts them into the release.
Operating systemArchitectureArchiveCarries its own ffmpeg
FreeBSDamd64rdio-scanner-freebsd-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linux386rdio-scanner-linux-386-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxamd64rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxarmrdio-scanner-linux-arm-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxarm64rdio-scanner-linux-arm64-v8.0.0.zipYes
macOSamd64rdio-scanner-macos-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
macOSarm64rdio-scanner-macos-arm64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Windowsamd64rdio-scanner-windows-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes

Every release carries the ffmpeg the audio conversion uses, embedded in the binary, so conversion works with nothing to install. The ffmpeg binaries are compiled for audio: the recipe disables every component and enables the audio demuxers, decoders, encoder, muxers and filters this server converts with, and the pipe, fd and file protocols a recording arrives and leaves on, so no video codec, decoder, or encoder, and no network protocol, is compiled into it. The Linux and Windows archives carry the ffmpeg binaries this project's build compiles, in a container, from the source release its manifest pins. The macOS and FreeBSD archives carry ffmpeg binaries compiled on the platform each target runs on, and this build compiles them on a machine that runs the target's operating system: the operating system is the rule, and the architecture inside it is not. The two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives, and Rosetta 2 is what lets it run the Intel programs it compiled; FreeBSD is compiled on FreeBSD, the one architecture FreeBSD is built for here. On the machine that is the target, one command — go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg — compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts. The compile is the check: the build runs the binaries it produced through the server's own conversions, asks them what they register, and adopts the ones that convert. On the other macOS architecture, go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 compiles the Intel binaries for the Intel archive, and the binaries a host compiles for the architecture it cannot run are left in the target's bundle directory for the Mac that runs them. Binaries you build by hand are adopted the same way — dropped in the target's bundle directory, and run by the build that adopts them — and the build adopts binaries on two things and nothing else: that the file holds the machine code the target runs, and that the binaries convert. The FFMPEG.txt beside the program says how the ffmpeg binaries the archive carries came to be.

Ports

The ports the server uses
PortWhat answers thereFlag
3000The main interface at /, the administration interface at /admin/, and every /api/ endpoint-listen (default :3000)

80 and 443Needed open to the world by the automatic certificate, which proves the domain owns the address-ssl_auto_cert

Recorders

Any recorder that writes one audio file per transmission works. What decides how the server reads the call's identity is the dirwatch type you choose, or the fields the recorder posts.

Recorders known to work, and the paths they use
RecorderUpload APIDirwatch
Trunk RecorderYesYes
RTLSDR-AirbandNoYes
SDRTrunkNoYes
voxcallYesNo
ProScanNoYes
DSDPlus Fast LaneNoYes

Worked recorder configurations, as the recorder's own configuration files, are in the repository under docs/examples/trunk-recorder and docs/examples/rtlsdr-airband. The worked configurations this guide carries are in chapter 10.

Machines

The server is a single Go binary and does not need much: a 1 GHz-class machine runs a small deployment comfortably, and a Raspberry Pi 3 or newer runs a typical one. Plan for disk, not for CPU: recordings accumulate, and the size of your database is the size of your retention. A deployment that keeps seven days of a busy system is measured in gigabytes, and the Prune days option is what bounds it.

The database is a requirement in its own right. SQLite needs nothing — the server writes one file in its data directory, which is the right choice for a single-instance deployment. MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL need a server you run and the connection flags that name it. See The database.

If you are building from source

  • Go 1.26 or newer.
  • Node.js 20 or newer, for the web applications the server carries inside it.
  • podman, or docker when podman is not there, for building the container image, and for compiling the ffmpeg of the five targets the build compiles one for. The build asks the machine which one it has and uses podman when it has both.
  • A C toolchain, and on FreeBSD gmake, to build the macOS and FreeBSD ffmpeg binaries: those are compiled by this build on a machine that runs the target's operating system, and that machine is a Mac for the two macOS targets — either architecture for either, since the two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries — or a FreeBSD box for the FreeBSD target. The five Linux and Windows ffmpeg binaries are compiled in a container, by the container program the build resolved, on the machine that produces the releases.

The build tool needs no configuration: it reads the release matrix, the version, and the ffmpeg bundle recipe from the repository. What it builds, and in what order, is what the four commands in chapter 4 show.

4 · Installation

Three ways to install: the precompiled archive for your platform, the container image, or the source. All three produce the same server; they differ in how you upgrade it and where its data lives.

From the precompiled archive

Download the archive for your platform and architecture from the releases page, and extract it where the server will live. An archive carries the program and the one document that operates it:

  • the rdio-scanner executable for your platform;
  • this guide, at docs/admin-guide.html;
  • FFMPEG.txt, the licence of the ffmpeg inside the program, and what it is: the ffmpeg binaries this project's build compiled — in a container for the Linux and Windows targets, on the machine that is the target for the macOS and FreeBSD ones — or the binaries its maintainer compiled on that platform and the build adopted.

The guide carries its own stylesheet and its own pictures, so an extracted archive needs nothing from the network and nothing from the repository. Put the folder somewhere the server can write: the server writes its database, its configuration file, and its state into the folder it was started from. 

cd /opt
unzip ~/Downloads/rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zip
cd rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0
./rdio-scanner

The per-system detail — where the server lives on that system, its service commands, its firewall, and what its archive contains — is in chapter 21, one sub-section for each of Linux, Windows, macOS, and FreeBSD.

From the container image

A container image is published for each release. The container serves from /app/data, so the data you must keep is whatever you mount there, and the mount must be writable by the user the container runs as: 

mkdir -p ~/.rdio-scanner

docker run --detach --name rdio-scanner \
    --env TZ=America/Toronto \
    --publish 3000:3000 \
    --restart always \
    --user $(id -u):$(id -g) \
    --volume ~/.rdio-scanner:/app/data \
    chuot/rdio-scanner:latest

Create the data folder before the first run. A folder the container daemon creates on your behalf is owned by the wrong user, and the server refuses a directory it cannot write — the same rule the server applies on a plain installation.

The compose file the project documents is the same run command written as a service: 

services:
  rdio-scanner:
    image: chuot/rdio-scanner:latest
    container_name: rdio-scanner
    environment:
      - TZ=America/Toronto
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    restart: always
    user: "1000:1000"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data

Two things an administrator running the container should know. The directory-watcher section is removed from the administration navigation when the server's environment names the container, because a watched directory inside a container is a container path and not yours — mount the recorder's folder into the container and watch the mount. And the container's data directory is /app/data, so the database file you back up is the one inside the mount: Backup and restore.

From source

With Go 1.26 and Node 20 installed, the build tool does the work: 

go run ./cmd/build client     # the web applications the server carries
go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg     # the ffmpeg of the platform you are on, compiled here
go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 # the Intel ffmpeg binaries, compiled on an Apple Silicon Mac
go run ./cmd/build server     # one binary, into dist/<target>/
go run ./cmd/build dist       # the release archive of this platform, into dist/
go run ./cmd/build dist --all # every release archive, into dist/
go run ./cmd/build container  # the container image, locally

server builds the web applications first, so the binary carries them and serves them with no separate web server. dist alone writes the archive of the platform you run it on; dist --all writes the archives for every platform in the release matrix: FreeBSD on amd64, Linux on 386, amd64, arm, and arm64, macOS on amd64 and arm64, and Windows on amd64. container builds the container image on the machine you run it on, for the architecture of that machine.

Every one of the eight builds carries its own ffmpeg, compiled for audio: the recipe the build tells the source disables every component and enables the audio components this server converts with, and the run that adopts binaries refuses binaries that register a video codec. The build compiles the five Linux and Windows targets itself, in a container, from the source release its manifest pins. The macOS and FreeBSD ffmpeg binaries are compiled on a machine that runs the target's operating system, and there the build compiles them itself: go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts, and the archive you build on that machine carries them. The compile is the check: the build runs the binaries it produced through the server's own conversions, asks them what they register, and adopts the ones that convert. The two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so an Apple Silicon Mac compiles the Intel binaries with go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64, and the binaries it compiles for the other architecture are run on the Mac that runs them: the run is the binaries' own execution, and Rosetta 2 is what lets an Apple Silicon Mac execute the Intel programs. The host that cannot run the binaries it compiled leaves them in the target's bundle directory, writes nothing down, and names the Mac that runs them and the command that compiles them there, so the arm64 binaries compiled on an Intel Mac are carried to an Apple Silicon Mac. The machine that produces the releases runs neither program, so a release run there skips those targets and ships the five archives it can ship, saying what would have made the rest buildable. Binaries you build by hand are adopted too, for the macOS and FreeBSD targets: drop ffmpeg and ffprobe in the target's bundle directory, and the build runs them and adopts what converts. The five targets this build compiles in a container take the binaries the container produced, and a program you drop in one of their directories is embedded in the binary and used by nothing. Nothing is copied out of a build and committed anywhere. The licence of the ffmpeg a release carries travels in that release, beside this guide.

The build tool takes the release name and an output path: --pre names a pre-release suffix carried in the version line the server reports, and -o sends the output somewhere other than dist/. go run ./cmd/build version prints the version the server will report, and clean takes the build's output away.

5 · First run

A fresh server needs one flag to run: it serves, creates its own database, and tells you in its console where it answers. The three things to do next are all in the administration interface, and the interface tells you what they are.

Starting it

./rdio-scanner

The server writes everything into its base directory: the executable's own folder, and when that folder is not writable, a folder named Rdio Scanner inside your home directory. -base_dir names a folder of your choosing instead, and that is the flag to set on a deployment you intend to keep. The server refuses to start when the base directory is not writable, and says so on the console.

On a first run the console says:

The two addresses are the same port by default: the listener interface at / and the administration interface at /admin/. The signing secret is how the server signs the sessions you open; it is generated once, stored in the database, and changing it ends every session that was open.

Logging in

Open http://localhost:3000/admin/ in a browser. The server ships with one administrator and the password rdio-scanner. Log in with it, and change it immediately — the interface tells you to, in the banner it shows you.

The login endpoint answers a token, and the browser keeps it for the session. The server signs tokens with its secret, keeps the last five it issued, and gives each one a seven-day life, so signing in ends the sessions older than that, and a session seven days old ends on its own. Three failed logins from one address lock that address out for ten minutes; the server logs the attempts under the login subsystem.

The banner that lists what is missing

The first page after login is a card that lists what a deployment still needs. It is computed from your configuration, so it clears itself as you work, and it names the control that clears each item:

The items the banner lists on a fresh deployment
LevelItemCleared by
WarningYou are using the default admin password, please change it from the tools / admin password menu.Tools ▸ Change password
InfoNo systems defined. Define one from the Systems menu, or turn on Options ▸ Auto Populate to have them created for you.The Systems section, or the Auto populate option
InfoNo apikeys or dirwatch defined. Set at least one to allow ingesting audio files.The API Keys section or the Dirwatch section

A first configuration, in order

  1. Change the administration password in Tools.
  2. Add a system in Systems — a system is the top of the hierarchy the listener browses.
  3. Give the recorder a way in: an API key for a recorder that posts calls, or a dirwatch for a recorder that writes files. See Getting audio in.
  4. Watch the Logs section while the first calls arrive. The ingest names the system and talkgroup it resolved, and says when it refused a call and why.

Each section saves with its own save bar, and the save is a write to the running server: the change is announced to every other open administration session, and the server files a the configuration changed entry in the log. Nothing needs a restart, except the flags.

Writing the flags to a file

Flags are read at start-up. Once you have the flags you want, -config_save writes them to rdio-scanner.ini in the base directory, and the server reads that file on every later start, so the flags no longer have to be repeated on the command line: 

./rdio-scanner -listen ":3000" -base_dir /opt/rdio-scanner -config_save
./rdio-scanner          # reads /opt/rdio-scanner/rdio-scanner.ini

The file is plain INI, one key = value per line, and it is the file to keep with your backup — it is the deployment's own shape, in text. Read the next chapter for which keys the file carries, and for the precedence the server applies between the file and the command line.

6 · Command line flags and the ini file

Flags decide the addresses the server answers on, the database it opens, and the TLS it serves. They are read once, at start-up, and -config_save writes them to a file so you stop typing them.

The flags

The table is the server's own flag set, transcribed from the composition root. Defaults are what the server uses when the flag is not given.

Every flag the server accepts
FlagDefaultWhat it decides
-admin_passwordnoneHash and store this password for the administrator, and stop without starting a server. The one flag that changes the credential from the command line. See the command line client.
-base_dirthe executable's folder, else ~/Rdio ScannerWhere the database file, the configuration file, and the server's state are written. Must be writable.
-bcrypt_cost10The bcrypt cost the administrator credential is hashed at, 10 to 14. A cost outside that range is refused at start-up.
-configrdio-scanner.iniThe name of the configuration file, read from the base directory.
-db_connect_timeoutnoneHow long the server waits for the database to answer, as a Go duration such as 5s.
-db_filerdio-scanner.dbThe SQLite database file, in the base directory.
-db_hostlocalhostThe database host, for MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
-db_namenoneThe database name, for MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
-db_passnoneThe database password.
-db_port3306, 5432 for PostgreSQLThe database host port.
-db_sslmodenoneThe PostgreSQL SSL mode, one of the PostgreSQL names such as disable, require, verify-full.
-db_tlsnoneThe MySQL and MariaDB TLS setting: true, false, skip-verify, or a registered TLS configuration name.
-db_typesqliteThe database backend: sqlite, mariadb, mysql, or postgresql. Anything else is refused at start-up.
-db_usernoneThe database user name.
-listen:3000The address the server answers on. :3000 listens on every address; 127.0.0.1:3000 listens on one.
-mcp_serverfalseServe the Model Context Protocol endpoint. See the MCP server.
-ssl_auto_certnoneA domain name to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for, automatically. Needs ports 80 and 443 reachable.
-ssl_cert_filenoneA PEM certificate to serve TLS with.
-ssl_key_filenoneThe PEM key that matches that certificate.
-ssl_listennoneThe address TLS is served on. Without it, TLS is served on the plain listening address when a certificate is configured.
-trusted_proxiesnoneComma-separated proxy addresses, CIDR or bare, whose X-Forwarded-For the server believes. See Reverse proxies.
The modes the same command line selects
FlagDefaultWhat it does
-cmdnoneDrive a server that is already running: log in, read and write the configuration, change the credential, add and remove listener accesses. It is a client of the public administration endpoints. See the command line client.
-config_savefalseWrite the configuration file and stop.
-servicenoneRun under the operating system's service manager: install, uninstall, start, stop, restart, and run as the service's own command. See Running as a service.
-versionfalsePrint the version and stop.

-h prints this list, and this table is the same list: where the two disagree, this table is the one the running server answers to.

The ini file, and which value wins

The server parses the command line, then reads rdio-scanner.ini from the base directory and overlays it. The file is plain INI, no section header, one key per line: 

db_type = postgresql
db_host = db.internal
db_name = rdioscanner
db_user = rdio
db_pass = <the password>
db_sslmode = require
listen = :3000
ssl_auto_cert = scanner.example.org
trusted_proxies = 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8
mcp_server = true
bcrypt_cost = 12

The keys the file can carry are:

bcrypt_cost, db_connect_timeout, db_file, db_host, db_name, db_pass, db_port, db_sslmode, db_tls, db_type, db_user, listen, mcp_server, ssl_auto_cert, ssl_cert_file, ssl_key_file, ssl_listen, trusted_proxies

The precedence is the detail that surprises people, so it is stated plainly: for a key the file names, the file wins; a key the file does not name leaves the command line's value alone. A missing or unreadable file leaves every flag as you typed it. -base_dir, -config, -admin_password, -cmd, -service, and -version are never read from the file: the base directory and the file name are how the server finds the file at all, and the rest are ways of running the program, not settings it runs with.

-config_save writes the file from the flags as parsed on that command line, prints rdio-scanner.ini file created, and stops. It writes the database keys for the backend you chose: a SQLite deployment writes db_file and db_type; a server-side backend writes host, name, user, password, TLS, SSL mode, connect timeout, port, and type. Because the file then outranks the command line, the usual path is: start once with the flags you want, add -config_save, and start the server with no flags at all.

The file holds secrets

The database password is in that file, in plain text. Restrict it — chmod 600 rdio-scanner.ini — and give the base directory to the user the server runs as and to nobody else. The administration password is not in the file: it is hashed in the database.

What the server refuses at start-up

Each of these stops the start, with the reason on the console, before a port is opened:

  • a base directory the server cannot write;
  • a -db_type outside the four supported backends;
  • a -bcrypt_cost outside 10 to 14 — a cost typo would hash the administrator credential at a cost you never asked for, and the credential on record is the one thing a typo must not touch;
  • a -db_connect_timeout that is not a duration.

A TLS listener that cannot start is the one failure that stops a server that was already answering: the plain address stops with it, and the log says the https address it could not answer. See TLS and HTTPS.

Environment variables

The variables the server reads
VariableEffect
DOCKERSet by the container image. It marks the deployment as containerised: the directory-watcher section is removed from the administration navigation, because a watched directory inside a container is a container path and not yours.
TZThe timezone the server's clock uses — log timestamps, and the day boundaries pruning works against. Set it explicitly on a container; the container's default is not your timezone.
RDIO_ADMIN_PASSWORDThe password -cmd login reads, so a script can log in without putting the credential in a command line the process list shows.

7 · The database

The server keeps its configuration, its recordings, and its log in one database. The choice of backend is a flag, the schema is the server's own, and an older database is migrated on the first start.

Backends

The backends the server answers to
BackendNeedsFlags that name it
sqlite (default)Nothing. One file in the base directory.-db_file
mariadbA MariaDB server you run and a database with a user.-db_host, -db_port, -db_name, -db_user, -db_pass, -db_tls
mysqlA MySQL server, the same way.the same, with -db_tls
postgresqlA PostgreSQL server.the same, with -db_sslmode in place of -db_tls

SQLite is the right answer for a single deployment: the whole server is one file, the server opens it with no network hop, and a backup is a copy. The server-side backends are the answer when the deployment shares the data with other systems, when the database is on its own host, or when your site's rules say the database must be a server. The port default is 3306, and 5432 when the type is PostgreSQL.

The server opens the database at start-up and refuses to start when it cannot reach it. A database that goes away while the server runs is reported in the log under the database subsystem, and the server recovers when the database comes back.

What is stored

What the server keeps in the database
StoredWhat it is
Systems, sites, talkgroups, unitsThe hierarchy a listener browses, and the identities the ingest resolves a call against.
Groups, tags, talkgroup groupsThe ways a listener and an access code select talkgroups across systems.
AccessesThe listener access codes: identity, the systems and talkgroups they reach, the expiry.
API keysThe keys a recorder posts calls with, and a downstream presents, each scoped to systems and talkgroups.
DirwatchesThe directories the server watches, their recorder type, and their mask.
DownstreamsThe other deployments calls are forwarded to, with the address and the key.
CallsEvery ingested transmission: its identity, its start and duration, its metadata, and its audio, stored in the database with the row.
Call frequencies, call patches, call unitsThe per-call detail a recorder reports: the frequency the call ran on, the talkgroups a patch involved, the units that took part.
DelayedThe calls the downstream delivery is holding before sending them.
LogsThe server's own log, read in the Logs section.
OptionsThe options, the signing secret, and the administrator credential's hash.
Migration archiveThe rows a migration read and could not carry, with the reason. See Upgrading and migrating.

The recordings are rows, not files. The base directory holds the database and the configuration file; the audio is inside the database, which is why a deployment is one file to back up, and why the database grows with your retention.

Retention

The retention pass deletes the calls and the log entries older than the Prune days option, calls first and the log after, and files what it removed under the prune subsystem: retention pass removed 1 234 calls and 5 678 log entries. Setting the option to 0 disables the pass, and the deployment keeps everything it has ever ingested.

The pass runs on the server's own schedule, against the server's clock, so the timezone matters on a deployment where the day boundary is meaningful. Pruning is not a backup: it is the opposite of one. Set the retention only after you have the backup you want.

When an older database is opened

A database written by an older server is migrated on the first start of this one: the schema is brought forward, the groups and tags the legacy server kept in the options are made into their own rows, and the log table is rebuilt. The rows the migration read and could not carry into the new shape are written to the migration archive with the table and row they came from, the reason, and the moment they were archived. Nothing is silently dropped.

The pass is re-run on the next start, and rows already archived archive as nothing rather than colliding, so a migration that stopped partway continues. Chapter 24 is the path for a version 5 deployment, and what to check after a migration.

Keeping it healthy

  • Back up the database file while the server is not writing to it, or take the backup from the database server's own tools. See Backup and restore.
  • Give the server-side backends a database user with the narrowest grant that lets the server work: the database, its tables, and nothing else.
  • Watch the database subsystem in the log. Connection failures, statements that failed, and the migration's own lines are filed there.
  • Do not edit the tables by hand. The administration interface is the path the server expects, and a hand-edited row is a row the server will read as its own.

8 · The administration interface

The interface at /admin/ is where a deployment is configured. It is one page served by the server, it edits the configuration through the running server, and it shows you what the server is doing while you work.

Logging in, and what a session is

The login sends the password to the server and the server answers a session token. The browser keeps that token for the session, and every request the interface makes carries it. The token is signed with the server's signing secret and is valid for seven days: the server keeps the last five tokens it issued, so a sixth sign-in ends the oldest session, a token past its seven days is refused, and a server that generates a new secret ends every session that was open before it.

Three failed logins from one address lock that address out for ten minutes. The server answers a refused login with the same message it answers a wrong password with — it never says how many attempts are left — and files the lockout in the log as too many login attempts from the address. Behind a reverse proxy, the address the server sees is the proxy's own unless you name the proxy as a trusted proxy: see Reverse proxies.

The navigation

The navigation lists the sections in the order an administrator works through a deployment: the Dashboard you land on, then the system and the sites, talkgroups, and units that belong to it, then the groups and tags a listener browses by, then the directory watches and downstreams that carry audio, then the API keys and access codes that say who may post calls and who may listen, then Options, then the Logs you watch while the first calls arrive, then the Tools, and the OpenAPI contract last because it is reference. Sections that answer the same question sit next to each other, so the sibling of what you are looking at is where you are already looking. On a narrow viewport the navigation sits above the content and the sections become a wrapping row, each item its icon beside its label.

The sections, and what each one configures
SectionWhat it carriesChapter
DashboardWhat the server is doing right now: how long it has been up, the listener connections it is holding, the directory watchers it started, the calls it recorded in the last 24 hours and the talkgroups busiest among them, and the errors and warnings its own log holds. It reads and never writes, and it is the section you land on after signing in.8
SystemsThe systems: each row's own fields, and the system's list of blacklisted talkgroup references.11
SitesThe sites of the system you have selected.11
TalkgroupsThe talkgroups of the system you have selected.11
UnitsThe units of the system you have selected.11
GroupsGroups of talkgroups, the way a listener selects many talkgroups at once.12
TagsTags, the labels a listener filters by.12
DirwatchThe directories the server watches for a recorder's files. Removed from the navigation when the server's environment names the container.10
DownstreamsThe other deployments calls are forwarded to.10
API KeysThe keys a recorder posts calls with, and a downstream presents.9
AccessListener access codes: who may listen, to which systems and talkgroups, until when.9
OptionsThe server's behaviour options.13
LogsThe server's own log, filtered and paged.14
ToolsExport and import the configuration, import talkgroups and units from CSV, change the password.15
OpenAPIEvery endpoint the server answers, read from the contract the server publishes.16

Sites, Talkgroups, and Units are the sub-sections of the system you have selected in Systems: they carry the system's name at their head, and their rows belong to that system.

The Dashboard is the section you land on after signing in, and it is the one section that reads and never writes: there is nothing on it to save and no field to fill. It shows what the server is doing at the moment you look at it — how long it has been up and what it is serving from, the listener connections it is holding, the directory watchers it started, the calls it recorded in the last 24 hours with the talkgroups busiest among them, and the errors and warnings its own log holds — and the line under the cards names the moment the server read them. The page asks the server again every five seconds; Auto-refresh turns that off, and Read again asks once, at the moment you ask. When the server stops answering, the dashboard takes its figures off the page rather than leave them there looking current, and says so out loud.

Rows, the save bar, and the conflict banner

Each section is a list of rows, and a row is collapsible: collapsed it shows the row's identity, expanded it shows every field it carries. In the Systems, Sites, Talkgroups, and Units sections one row is open at a time: opening a row closes the rows that were open, and the section's add control opens the row it creates, so the list stays short and the save bar stays within reach. The Tools panels and the OpenAPI endpoint rows open side by side. Add a row with the section's add control, delete it with the row's own delete button. Nothing is written while you type.

The save bar at the bottom of a section is what writes your work. It is enabled when the section has unsaved changes and they are valid, and it says what is unsaved. Save sends the section to the running server; Discard throws the unsaved work away and reloads the section as the server has it.

Two sessions editing the same section is the case the conflict banner is for. When another session saved the section while you were editing it, the banner appears above the list with Reload from server and Discard: reload takes the server's current version and lets you re-apply your change on top of it, and discarding your work is the honest way out of a collision you did not want. Saving over another administrator's work is what the banner exists to stop.

A save is a write to the running server, and the server tells every other open administration session that the configuration changed, over the connection the interface holds open for exactly that. The server files the configuration changed in the log. No restart is involved: the sections are live. The flags are not — see the flags chapter.

The systems-and-talkgroups dialog

Access codes and API keys are scoped to systems and talkgroups, and Downstreams are scoped the same way for what they send. The control that picks the scope opens the same dialog in all three sections: the systems, each with its talkgroups, with a control per system and per talkgroup, and the groups and tags named where they apply.

What the interface tells you

  • The banner at the top of the page lists what the deployment is missing, and clears itself as you clear the items. It is on the first run.
  • A snackbar confirms what just happened — a save, an export, a password change — at the bottom of the page.
  • The Logs section is the server's own account of what it did, and it is where a problem is diagnosed. It is on the log chapter.
  • The OpenAPI section is the endpoint list the server publishes, with the authentication each endpoint takes.

The container changes one thing

When the server's environment names the container, the Dirwatch section is not in the navigation. A watched directory inside a container is a container path, and the recorder writing it is outside the container: the section would invite you to configure a path the server cannot see. Run the container with the recorder's folder mounted, and watch the mount. The container installation is the place that sets this up.

9 · Access codes and API keys

Two credentials leave a deployment: the access code a listener presents to hear the audio, and the API key a capture box presents to deliver it. They are separate lists, they are scoped the same way, and they are checked at different moments — one when a listener connects, the other when a recording arrives.

The two credentials, and where each one is presented
CredentialWho holds itPresented atUnlocks
Access codeA listenerThe listener application's access code prompt, and the X-Access-Code header on the call history endpointsThe live feed, and the recorded calls inside its scope
API keyA recorder, a capture box, another Rdio Scanner deploymentThe key field of an upload, and the API key field of a downstream, which is the key that deployment's server acceptsThe right to post calls, inside its scope

Access codes

An access code is a listener's permission to watch the server. The row carries the code itself, a name the log and the interface show, the moment the code stops working, how many listeners may use it at the same time, and the systems and talkgroups it unlocks.

The access code row
FieldWhat it is for
CodeThe credential. Required. The field is masked; the eye button next to it reveals it so an administrator can read it out to someone over the phone.
IdentThe name the log and the interface show for this code. It is what a log entry about an expired or locked code names.
ExpirationA date and time. Leave it empty and the code never expires. Once the moment has passed, the code is refused and the listener is told its access has expired.
LimitHow many listeners may hold this code at the same time. 0 or empty means no cap. A listener arriving at the cap is refused and told so.
Choose systemsOpens the scope dialog: Everything, Groups, Tags, or the systems and talkgroups you tick.
Delete accessRemoves the row. Nothing is written until you save the section.

An open server and a restricted one

The Access section decides which kind of server you are running. An empty access list is an open server: every listener is given the whole configuration and is never asked for a code. A list with one entry in it is a restricted server, and every listener must present a code before the server sends it anything.

That is the whole switch, and it is worth being deliberate about. Adding the first access code changes a server that anyone could listen to into one that answers nobody until they present a code — including the applications that were listening a minute ago.

What a listener is told

The server checks a code in a fixed order, and the order is visible to the listener, so it is worth knowing before someone phones you about it.

The listener's outcomes, in the order the server checks them
OutcomeWhat the listener seesWhat the log files
Attempts spentThe code prompt again, and nothing else is examined — a correct code arriving after the attempts are spent is refusedNothing: the attempts are counted, not recorded
Code not on the listThe code prompt againa listener from the address presented an access code that is not valid, once per window, not once per guess
Valid code on the last allowed attemptThe code prompt, and the code is refusedthe access code for ident … is locked after too many attempts
Expired codeThe access has expiredthe access code for ident … has expired
Limit reachedThe connection limit is reachedident … is already at its limit of N listeners, and the connection was refused
AcceptedThe live feed starts, with the configuration the scope allowsNothing. A listener joining is a Live feed entry, not a login entry

Five attempts is the limit, counted twice over: once for the session and once for the address it came from. A code that is accepted clears both counters. A code that is refused does not, whichever reason refused it, which is what makes the counter a limit on trying rather than a limit on being wrong.

A code is a credential, so the server never writes one in its log. The entry that names a refused code names the address it came from, and the entry that names an expired or locked code names the ident — never the code. A guessing tool must not be able to fill the log view, which is why the warning about an invalid code is said once per window and not once per guess.

API keys

An API key is the credential an ingest source posts calls with. It carries the key itself, a name, a switch that turns it off without deleting it, and the systems and talkgroups it may upload to.

The API key row
FieldWhat it is for
DisabledTurns the key off. A disabled key uploads nothing, and the row stays where it is so you can turn it back on.
KeyThe credential. Required. The copy button next to it puts it on the clipboard, which is what you paste into the recorder's configuration.
IdentThe name for this key.
Choose systemsOpens the same scope dialog an access code uses.
Delete API keyRemoves the row.

A key you add with the section's add control starts scoped to Everything. A key whose scope is empty uploads nothing, so a key you have scoped to systems and then unticked everything under is a key that has stopped working — the upload is refused, and the log says the key is not valid.

Where the key goes depends on the ingest path. A watched directory needs no key at all — the directory is the credential, which is why watched directories are yours to protect. An upload to /api/call-upload carries the key in the key form field of the multipart request, and a trunk-recorder upload carries it in the same field. A downstream carries the key the other server accepts, in its API key field.

An upload the server refuses is answered 401 with the plain text Access denied, and the refusal is filed in the log as the apikey is not valid — the recorder gets the same text it has always got, and you have a record of the box that reached the server and was turned away.

The scope dialog

Access codes, API keys, and downstreams all open the same dialog, because the server scopes all three against the same two things: a system and a talkgroup.

  • Everything is the whole deployment: every system, every talkgroup, and every one added later.
  • Groups and Tags tick a whole group or tag at once. A box in its third state means the scope covers part of that group, which is what a group you ticked and then narrowed inside the Systems list looks like.
  • Systems lists each system with its talkgroups under it. Ticking a system ticks its talkgroups; unticking one talkgroup leaves the rest.

A system in the scope with no talkgroups named under it is not in the scope at all. That is the shape of the stored scope, and it is the one thing about the dialog that bites: a system whose talkgroup list is empty grants nothing, so a listener holding that scope sees a live feed with nothing in it and an upload to that system is refused.

For a downstream, the scope is not what the downstream may see — it is the calls this server forwards to it. A downstream scoped to two systems forwards those systems' calls and nothing else, and a downstream with no scope forwards nothing.

The dialog is on the administration interface chapter, photographed with the groups and tags named.

Scoping is a grant, not a filter. A listener whose scope covers a talkgroup can hear it; a listener whose scope does not cannot, and there is no setting on the listener's side that changes that. When someone reports a talkgroup they cannot hear, the answer is in that listener's scope, and the summary line under Choose systems — all systems and talkgroups or some — is where you start.

10 · Getting audio in

Audio arrives in one of three ways: the server watches a directory the recorder writes into, a recorder posts a call to an upload endpoint, or another Rdio Scanner deployment forwards its calls here. A deployment usually runs one of the first two, and the choice is a matter of where the recorder sits relative to the server.

The three ingest paths, and when each one is the right one
PathNeedsUse it when
DirwatchA directory both the recorder and the server can reach, and the server's own file accessThe recorder writes on the same machine, or on a share the server can read
Upload endpointAn API key, and a recorder that can post to the server's addressThe recorder is on another host, another site, or behind a box you cannot mount
DownstreamThe other deployment's address and an API key valid thereTwo deployments, and one of them should carry the other's calls

Dirwatch

A dirwatch is a directory the server watches, plus the instructions for reading the files that appear in it. The row says which recorder writes there, because the recorder decides how a file's metadata is written — in the file name, in the path, in the MP3 tags, or in a sidecar JSON file.

The dirwatch row
FieldWhat it is for
DirectoryThe directory to watch. The recorder's own output directory: Record, 1R-Record, or VC-Record for DSDPlus Fast Lane, Recordings for SDRTrunk, captureDir for Trunk Recorder, and any directory you point a recorder at for the default type.
TypeHow a file's metadata is read. See the table below.
ExtensionThe audio extension to watch, without the period: mp3, wav.
System, Site, TalkgroupSend everything in this directory to a fixed system, site, and talkgroup, whatever the file says. Leave them empty and the metadata read from the file decides.
MaskFor the default type: the pattern that reads the metadata out of the file name. See the tokens below.
FrequencyA fake frequency in hertz shown on the listener's screen, for a recorder that reports none.
DelayMilliseconds a file is allowed to settle before the server reads it, for a recorder that writes the sidecar after the audio. The default is 2000. A delay longer than a day is clamped to a day.
Delete afterDelete the files once the call is built, so the watched directory does not fill up. On by default.
DisabledStops watching this directory without deleting the row.

A watched directory must be a local directory. Dirwatch is not compatible with networked disk: a watch over a network mount misses files, reads them half-written, and reports failures you cannot fix from the server. Put the recorder's output on the server's own disk, and in a container, watch the mount, not the recorder's path.

The four recorder types

What each type reads a call's metadata from
TypeMetadata comes fromWhat you set
DefaultThe file name, read with a mask you writeMask, extension, and the system, site, and talkgroup overrides
DSDPlus Fast LaneThe file path: the folder names under the record directory name the system, talkgroup, and unitThe directory, and nothing else
SDRTrunkThe MP3 tags SDRTrunk writes from its aliases tabThe directory and the extension
Trunk RecorderThe JSON sidecar Trunk Recorder writes beside the audio fileThe directory, and the extension

The mask tokens

A mask is the file name written with tokens standing in for the parts you want read. The server replaces each token with a pattern, matches the file name against the result, and assigns the captured pieces to the values the tokens name. The order the tokens appear in the mask is the order the pieces appear in the name.

Every mask token
TokenReads
#DATEThe date: 20201231, 2020-12-31, 2020_12_31
#TIMEThe local time: 085343, 08-34-39, 08:34:39
#ZTIMEThe same shape of time, read as the call's instant in the server's zone
#SYSThe system identifier, decimal, as the recorder numbers it
#SYSLBLThe system label
#SITEThe site identifier
#SITELBLThe site label
#TGThe talkgroup identifier, decimal
#TGLBLThe talkgroup label
#TGAFSThe talkgroup identifier in agency-fleet-subfleet form, 11-061
#GROUPThe group label
#TAGThe tag label
#UNITThe unit identifier
#UNITLBLThe unit label
#HZA frequency in hertz, 119100000
#KHZA frequency in kilohertz, 119100
#MHZA frequency in megahertz, 119.100
#TGHZA frequency in hertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119100000 becomes talkgroup 119100
#TGKHZA frequency in kilohertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119100.000 becomes talkgroup 119100
#TGMHZA frequency in megahertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119.100000 becomes talkgroup 119100

A mask for a conventional recorder that names the talkgroup by its frequency is therefore cymx_#TG_#DATE_#TIME_#HZ, and for the airband recorder below, laurentides_#DATE_#TIME_#TGHZ.

A mask is compiled as a regular expression, and two things about it are worth knowing. A mask that is not a valid expression is refused when you save the section, so a stray bracket never reaches the watcher. And a mask whose groups do not line up with the tokens it names is reported when the watch starts — the watcher says the mask captures more pieces than it names, which is the shape of a call built with the wrong values in it.

Uploading a call

Two endpoints take a call as a multipart form. Both answer plain text, and both answer the same way whatever the server then makes of the call: a call that was accepted is answered Call imported successfully., and a call the credentials refuse is answered 401 with Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>.

The upload endpoints
EndpointWhat it takesUse it for
POST /api/call-uploadA multipart body: the credential in the key field, the recording in the audio field, and the metadata in the fields belowA recorder, a script, or an integration that names the call's fields itself
POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-uploadA multipart body: key, the recording in audio, and Trunk Recorder's JSON sidecar in metaDeprecated. Trunk Recorder on a host the server cannot watch, until it posts to the endpoint above

The trunk-recorder endpoint is deprecated in favor of /api/call-upload, and a future release will remove it. It exists because Trunk Recorder posts a JSON sidecar beside the recording and that endpoint reads the sidecar as a document; the general endpoint reads form fields, and a call it takes is the same call. Moving a recorder means reading the sidecar and posting what is in it as the fields below — system, talkgroup, frequency, site, timestamp, audio, and the rest — beside the key. A meta part posted to the general endpoint is not read as a sidecar: it is one more form field, and the call arrives without what was in it.

Nothing else about the upload changes: the same key, the same plain-text answers, the same ingest. Plan the move while the endpoint is answering, and do not let a recorder you no longer run be the one that finds out it is gone.

The fields /api/call-upload reads
FieldMeaning
keyThe API key. The upload is refused when it is missing, disabled, or scoped away from the call.
audioThe recording, as a file part. Its name and content type are taken from the part.
audioFilename, audioNameThe name to file the recording under, and the type its extension implies
audioMime, audioTypeThe recording's content type
audioLengthThe recorder's own length in seconds. The server takes its word and measures nothing.
timestampThe call's instant, RFC 3339
dateTimeThe same instant under its pre-v7 name, as a Unix second count or an RFC 3339 string
system, site, talkgroupThe identifiers, as the recorder numbers them. These are matched against the identifiers your configuration uses.
systemLabel, talkgroupLabel, talkgroupNameThe labels, used to find the system and talkgroup when no identifier matched, and to name a talkgroup auto populate creates
talkgroupGroup, talkgroupGroupsThe group labels for a talkgroup auto populate creates
talkgroupTagThe tag label for a talkgroup auto populate creates
frequency, frequenciesOne frequency, or a JSON list of them with freq, dbm, pos, errorCount, and spikeCount
source, unitsThe unit identifier, or a JSON list of units with their offsets
patches, patched_talkgroupsThe talkgroup identifiers patched into this call
channelTypetrunked or conventional. Shown on the live frame for a call happening now; nothing else acts on it.

Every field is optional and each is read on its own, so a field the server does not know is read as nothing and the rest of the upload still lands. A call the server cannot place — no system matches, no talkgroup matches, auto populate switched off — is answered as accepted all the same, and the reason lands in the log under Call ingest. That is the first place to look when a capture box says it uploaded and the call is nowhere to be found.

Trunk Recorder on another host

Trunk Recorder's uploadScript property runs a script for each finished call, with the system identifier as its first argument and the recording's full path as its second. This is the script the repository carries; it posts the recording and its sidecar and then removes them. 

#!/bin/bash
#
# Use this script with Trunk Recorder's uploadScript system property in its
# config.json file:
#
#   {
#     ...
#     "uploadScript": "upload-call.sh 7537"
#     ...
#   }
#
# The first argument is the Rdio Scanner system identifier; Trunk Recorder adds
# the full path of the audio file as the second argument.

# The API key configured in your Rdio Scanner instance.
apikey=b29eb8b9-9bcd-4e6e-bb4f-d244ada12736

basename="${2%.*}"

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/trunk-recorder-call-upload \
     -F "key=${apikey}" \
     -F "audio=@${basename}.wav;type=audio/wav" \
     -F "meta=@${basename}.json;type=application/json" \
     -F "system=${1:-0}"

# The audio file and its JSON sidecar are then deleted.
rm -f ${basename}.*

Change the key and the address, and give Trunk Recorder your system's identifier. When the recorder and the server are on the same host, watch the capture directory instead — a dirwatch needs no key, no script, and no network.

This script posts to the deprecated endpoint. The same call goes to /api/call-upload as form fields, with the values the sidecar carries named for what they are: 

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/call-upload \
     -F "key=${apikey}" \
     -F "audio=@${basename}.wav;type=audio/wav" \
     -F "system=${1:-0}" \
     -F "talkgroup=${talkgroup}" \
     -F "frequency=${frequency}" \
     -F "site=${site}" \
     -F "timestamp=${timestamp}"

The sidecar's own names are the field names above, so the move is reading the JSON and naming the fields, not translating the call. The fields the general endpoint reads are listed above, and the endpoint answers the same two lines either way.

RTLSDR-Airband

RTLSDR-Airband writes one file per transmission into a directory, naming the file from a template and appending the frequency when include_freq is on. The server reads that name with a mask, so what you set up is a recorder configuration and a dirwatch row. 

devices: (
  {
    type = "rtlsdr";
    serial = "00000081";
    gain = 22.9;
    centerfreq = 119.1;
    channels: (
      {
        freq = 119.1;
        lowpass = 2500;
        highpass = 250;
        modulation = "am";
        outputs: (
          {
            type = "file";
            directory = "/tmp/recorders/Laurentides";
            filename_template = "laurentides";
            split_on_transmission = true;
            include_freq = true;
          }
        );
      }
    );
  }
);

And the dirwatch row that reads it:

The dirwatch row for the airband recorder above
FieldValue
Directory/tmp/recorders/Laurentides
Extensionmp3
TypeDefault
SystemThe system the channels belong to
Masklaurentides_#DATE_#TIME_#TGHZ

#TGHZ is what makes this work: it reads the frequency out of the name and sets the talkgroup identifier from it, so each frequency RTLSDR-Airband records becomes its own talkgroup without you listing one per channel.

Downstreams

A downstream is another Rdio Scanner deployment this one re-posts its calls to. The row carries the address to post to, the API key that deployment accepts, a switch, and the scope of the calls to forward.

The downstream row
FieldWhat it is for
URLThe other deployment's address. Only http and https are accepted, and the row is refused at save with any other scheme: the server posts your recordings and the key to this address, so it will not post them over something else.
API keyThe key the other server has in its API Keys section. A key from this server means nothing there.
DisabledStops forwarding without deleting the row.
Choose systemsThe calls to forward. A downstream with no scope forwards nothing.

Forwarding is a delivery, and it is logged as one: the Downstreams subsystem names the system, the talkgroup, the destination, and the outcome. When a call was recorded here and never appeared there, that entry is the answer, and the usual causes are a key that is disabled on the far side, a scope that does not cover the talkgroup, and an address that does not answer.

Auto populate

Auto populate is what makes a deployment that receives calls it has no configuration for keep working. It is a server-wide option and a per-system switch, and they do different things.

What auto populate creates, and which switch decides
CreatedEnabled byNamed from
A systemThe server-wide option onlyThe identifiers and label the call claims
A talkgroupThe server-wide option, or that system's own switchThe identifiers and labels the call claims; a talkgroup with no labels joins the group Unknown and the tag Untagged
UnitsThe server-wide option, or that system's own switchThe unit identifiers the call names

Each creation is a Configuration log entry naming the recording that caused it, so a system that appeared on its own is traceable to the file that named it. A system's Blacklists field is the counterweight: a comma-separated list of talkgroup references whose calls that system refuses. The refusal is not part of auto populate and does not depend on it: every call whose system and talkgroup resolve is refused when the talkgroup's reference is in the list, auto populate enabled or not. A talkgroup the operator configured is therefore refused outright, and one auto populate invents is accepted for the call that invents it — nothing in the list is configured yet for that call to be matched against — and refused from the next call on. The Talkgroups section carries a Blacklist talkgroup button that appends the talkgroup's reference to its system's list and removes its row, so the list is edited where the talkgroup is: the click stores the rows that are left together with the list, and the Systems section shows the entry after it. A section holding a talkgroup row the page will not save is refused, and says which fields to fix. The Systems section saves the list the server holds, so saving a system after blacklisting one of its talkgroups keeps the entry; a list the operator was writing in the Systems section's own Blacklists field and had not saved is replaced by the entry the click stores, and the click says so.

Auto populate is a good default for a deployment that follows a system as it grows, and a nuisance on a deployment with a fixed list: a capture box with a broken configuration fills a database with talkgroups nobody named. The per-system switch is what a deployment that mostly runs a fixed list wants.

11 · Systems, sites, talkgroups, and units

The configuration has one spine. A system is the trunked system or the conventional network the recorder captures; under it are its sites, its talkgroups, and its units. Everything the server files a recording against, and everything a listener selects, sits on that spine.

Systems is its own section. Sites, Talkgroups, and Units are the sub-sections of the system you have selected: each names the system at its head, and the rows you add there belong to it.

Systems

The system row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe system identifier, in decimal, as your recorder numbers it. This is the identifier a recorder's metadata is matched against, and the one an access code's scope names.
LabelThe name listeners see, on the main screen and in the search panel.
TypeThe system's modulation or trunking standard: AM, DMR, FM, NFM, NXDN, P25, Provoice, SmartNet, Tetra, or no type. It is shown with the system; nothing in the server's behaviour depends on it.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call assigned to this system. The alerts are the named oscillator sequences the server knows; they are listed in chapter 16.
Led ColorThe colour a listener's display shows for this system's calls. The default is green.
Auto PopulateCreates this system's talkgroups and units when a recording names ones you have not configured. It works beside the server-wide option: see auto populate.
DelayMinutes this system's calls are held before they are propagated to listeners.
BlacklistsA comma-separated list of talkgroup references this system refuses: every call whose system and talkgroup resolve is refused when the talkgroup's reference is in the list, auto populate enabled or not. The Blacklist talkgroup action of the Talkgroups section appends a reference here and stores it with that talkgroup's rows in the click. This section saves the list the server holds: saving a system after blacklisting one of its talkgroups keeps the entry, and a list you were writing in this field and had not saved is replaced by the entry the click stores, which the click tells you.

Rows are dragged into the order listeners see them in, and the order is saved with the section. A system's rows are deleted with the row's own button, and deleting a system takes its sites, talkgroups, and units with it.

Sites

A site is a transmitter location within a system. The row carries the recorder's site identifier and the label listeners see, and the sites of a system are dragged into order like everything else.

Talkgroups

A talkgroup is what a listener selects and what a recording is filed against. It carries the recorder's identifier, the label and name shown on the listener's screen, the groups it belongs to, the tag it carries, its alert and colour, its type, a fake frequency, and its own delay.

The talkgroup row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe talkgroup identifier, in decimal, as the recorder numbers it.
LabelThe label shown on the main screen and on the listener's buttons.
NameThe name shown on the main screen, beside the label.
GroupsThe groups this talkgroup belongs to, ticked in place. A talkgroup in no group is selected on its own and nowhere else.
TagThe one tag this talkgroup carries, chosen from the Tags section.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to this talkgroup's calls.
Led ColorThe colour this talkgroup's calls show in a listener's display.
TypeThe talkgroup's channel type, shown to listeners.
FrequencyA fake frequency in hertz shown on the main screen, for a talkgroup the recorder reports no frequency for.
DelayMinutes this talkgroup's calls are held before they are propagated to listeners.
Blacklist talkgroupAppends this talkgroup's reference to its system's blacklist and removes the row from the section, so the server stops taking calls on it: the click stores the removal and the new entry in one save, and the Systems section shows the entry after it. A section holding a talkgroup row the page will not save is refused, and says which fields to fix. The list itself lives on the system row, where the Systems section shows it as text in its Blacklists field and saves the list the server holds; a list left unsaved in that field is replaced by this entry, and the click says so.

Units

A unit is a radio the calls are attributed to. The row carries the identifier the recorder names, the label the listener sees, and an identifier range.

The unit row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe unit identifier, in decimal, as the recorder names it.
Range from, Range toA range of identifiers this one row covers, so a fleet of identifiers that share a label is written as one row.
LabelThe name the listener sees for the unit.

Identifiers, and how a recording finds its talkgroup

Every one of these rows carries an identifier that belongs to your recorder, not to the database. The server keeps its own identifiers, and the row's Id is the reference the recorder and the listener applications use. When a recording arrives, the server looks for the system and the talkgroup in a fixed order:

  1. the database identifier, when the upload names one;
  2. then the recorder identifier you typed into the row;
  3. then the label, when the recording names a system or talkgroup by name.

Nothing is created by that lookup on its own — that is auto populate's job, and it is a separate decision. A recording that matches nothing is a Call ingest log entry naming the recording, which is where a capture box that stopped appearing is diagnosed.

Two rows carrying the same identifier in one system is a deployment that files calls against whichever row the lookup reaches first. The interface marks the second row Id is already defined and keeps the section's Save disabled until you fix it; the server's own endpoint does not refuse the identifier, so a configuration written through the API can carry the duplicate. When calls land on a talkgroup with a label you did not expect, the duplicate identifier is what to look for.

Alerts, colours, and which one wins

Alert tones and LED colours are set at four levels — group, tag, system, talkgroup — and the assignment order is group, then tag, then system, then talkgroup. A talkgroup in a group that carries an alert takes the group's alert, whatever its system says. The colour works the same way, and the default colour is green.

Importing the list

A talkgroup and unit list from another application is imported as CSV, from the Tools section, per system. It is on the tools chapter, with the columns it takes.

12 · Groups and tags

A group is how a listener selects many talkgroups at once. A tag is a label on a talkgroup that a listener filters by. Both carry an alert tone and a colour that win over the system and the talkgroup, and both are used as scope shortcuts when an access code is written.

Groups

A group is a named collection of talkgroups. The group row is short: a label, an alert, and a colour. The talkgroups join it from the Talkgroups section, where the groups are ticked on each talkgroup row.

The group row
FieldWhat it is for
LabelRequired. The name shown on the listener's main screen, in the search panel, and in the select panel.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call assigned to this group. It wins over the system's and the talkgroup's alert.
Led ColorThe colour this group's calls show, winning over the system's colour. The default is green.
Delete GroupRemoves the group. The talkgroups that were in it stay, and become members of no group.

A talkgroup must belong to at least one group: the interface marks a talkgroup with no group Group is required and keeps the section's Save disabled until one is ticked. A deployment that groups nothing is a deployment whose listeners select talkgroups one at a time.

Tags

A tag is a label a talkgroup carries — Fire, EMS, Dispatch — and a talkgroup carries one tag at most, chosen on the talkgroup row.

The tag row
FieldWhat it is for
LabelRequired. The name shown on the listener's main screen and in the search panel.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call on a talkgroup carrying this tag. It wins over the system's and the talkgroup's alert, and loses to the group's.
Led ColorThe colour calls on a talkgroup with this tag show, winning over the system's colour.
Delete TagRemoves the tag. Talkgroups that carried it are left untagged.

Groups and tags in the rest of the deployment

Where groups and tags are used
Used byHow
The listener's select panelA group is selected as one item, and brings its talkgroups with it.
The scope dialogGroups and Tags are the two shortcuts for writing an access code's, an API key's, or a downstream's scope: ticking a group ticks its talkgroups. See the scope dialog.
Alerts and coloursThe assignment order is group, then tag, then system, then talkgroup.
Auto populateA talkgroup created from a recording that names no group joins the group Unknown and carries the tag Untagged. A recording that names group and tag labels creates them under those names.
The logA group, tag, or talkgroup the server created because a recording named it is a Configuration entry naming the recording.

Groups and tags are the two scope shortcuts that survive a system's growth. An access code scoped to a group covers the talkgroups added to that group later; a code scoped to a list of talkgroups covers exactly the ones you ticked. For a deployment whose listeners follow a system as it grows, groups are the scope that keeps working.

13 · Options

Options are the settings that describe how the server behaves rather than what it contains: audio conversion, auto populate, the listener cap, retention, duplicate detection, and the text a listener sees on the main screen. They are saved like any other section, and they take effect without a restart.

The options, with their defaults
OptionDefaultWhat it does
Audio ConversionEnabled without normalizationConverts an ingested recording to AAC in an m4a container at 32 kbit/s with ffmpeg, so a recording in any format the recorder writes plays in a browser. See the modes below.
Auto PopulateOnGlobally allows the creation of systems, talkgroups, and units a recording names that you have not configured. The per-system switch is on a system row. See auto populate.
Branding LabelEmptyA line of text shown above the listener's main screen, to identify which instance a listener is looking at.
Disable Duplicate Call DetectionOff, so detection is onStops the server discarding a recording that duplicates the one before it: two calls on the same system, talkgroup, and site within half a second are the same call. The window is fixed at 500 milliseconds.
Email SupportEmptyThe address listeners are pointed to when they need support.
Keypad Beep StyleUnidenThe tones a listener's keypad actions synthesize: the Uniden set or the Whistler set.
Max Clients200How many listener connections the server holds at once. A listener arriving when the cap is reached has its connection closed, with nothing said on it.
Prune Days7How long the call history and the log are kept. The retention pass runs once an hour. 0 switches retention off, and a deployment with retention off writes no retention entry.
Show Listeners CountOffShows how many listeners are connected, on the main screen and in the live feed.
Sort TalkgroupsOffSorts the talkgroup lists by identifier, instead of the order you dragged them into.

Audio conversion, in its four modes

The audio conversion modes
ModeWhat the server does with a recording
DisabledStores the recording exactly as it arrived and runs nothing. A recording the browser cannot play is a recording the listener cannot play.
Enabled without normalizationConverts to AAC at 32 kbit/s. Loudness is whatever the recorder captured.
Enabled with normalizationConverts, and applies ffmpeg's loudness normalization to the result, with a three-second pad so a short transmission is not clipped by the filter.
Enabled with loud normalizationThe same, with the loudness target fixed: −16 LUFS integrated, −1.5 dBTP true peak, 11 LU loudness range. This is the mode for a deployment whose recordings come from recorders with wildly different gains.

Two things about conversion are worth knowing before you rely on it. The normalization modes need a ffmpeg built with the loudnorm filter; the server checks the program it has at startup, and a build without the filter converts in the plain mode whatever the option says. And the tags written into the converted file — the album, artist, date, genre, and title a recording carries when a listener downloads it — are written only for a talkgroup that has a tag.

A recording is never lost because its audio would not convert. When ffmpeg is not installed, the server says so once and stores recordings as they arrived. When ffmpeg refuses a file, the server files what ffmpeg said under Audio conversion and stores the recording as it arrived. The conversion is a step after the call is filed, and a deployment with a broken ffmpeg keeps its calls.

Retention

Prune Days is the deployment's memory: the call history, the recordings, and the log entries older than that many days are removed by a pass that runs once an hour. It is the option that decides whether a deployment fills its disk, and the Retention subsystem is where you check that it is running. The detail is on the log chapter.

What is not in Options

The administrator password and the server's signing secret live in the options table and are not controls on this section: the password is changed in the Tools section, on the tools chapter.
