The flags — the address the server answers on, the database it opens, TLS, the service — are not options either, and they are set at startup: the flags chapter.

Options are saved as a section, and the section is written whole. Two administrators in the Options section is the case the conflict banner is for: the banner appears when the other session saved while you were editing, and Reload from server is the answer. See the administration interface.

14 · Logs

The server writes down what it does, and every entry says which part of the server wrote it. On a deployment that is misbehaving you do not read everything the server said: you ask for what the directory watchers said, or what the last hour of logins said, and read only that.

The log is in three places, and it is the same log

  • the Logs section of the administration interface, at /admin/;
  • the server's console, which is what journalctl -u rdio-scanner shows on a service deployment;
  • the logs table of the database.

The levels are Informative, Warning, and Error. A line that only ever went to the console — the base folder the server serves, the server stopping, a new signing secret, and everything the server said about a listener connection it could not read, could not understand, or could not write to — is written to the log as well, so it is searchable instead of something you had to be watching when it happened. The three notices that name the addresses the server is listening on are console only: they say where to point a browser, not what the server did.

A stored message says what happened, in the language of the system, and where something failed the failure's own text follows it. On the console and in the service log the same entry carries its level and its subsystem in front of it, so the subsystem split reaches the deployments diagnosed from a terminal: 

warn dirwatch: the watcher for /data/rdio/watch/trunk stopped: no such file or directory

That is what you grep for: journalctl -u rdio-scanner | grep ' dirwatch: '.

The subsystems

The names are a closed list. Asking the log view for a subsystem the server does not have is answered as a bad request, not as an empty log: an empty log would tell you nothing happened, when what happened is that you asked for something this server cannot report.

Every subsystem the server files entries under, and what it reports
SubsystemShown asWhat it covers
serverServerThe server starting, the base folder it serves, and the server stopping — including an address it could not stop answering.
configConfigurationA configuration you saved, a configuration that could not be saved, and a system, talkgroup, group, tag, or unit the server created because a recording named it.
dirwatchDirectory watchersThe watched recording directories: starting a watch, losing one, reading one, and handing a recording to the ingest path.
downstreamDownstreamsSending a call to another Rdio Scanner deployment.
delayerDelayed callsCalls held back by the Delayed feature: holding one, releasing one, and failing to do either.
ingestCall ingestA recording becoming a call, and a recording that matches no system or talkgroup the server knows.
loginLoginsA refused attempt, too many attempts from one address, a sign-in or sign-out the server could not carry out. A sign-in that worked writes nothing: the administration interface's own connection records that an administrator arrived, under Administration.
accessAccess codesA client presenting an access code that is not valid, expired, locked, or already at its connection limit.
livefeedLive feedListeners joining and leaving, how many there are, and what the server could not read from or write to one.
ffmpegAudio conversionConverting a recording to playable audio. The entry carries what the converter said, and the reason is at the end of it.
uploadUploadsAn upload the server refused, and the reason it refused it — the text the recorder gets back.
pruneRetentionThe retention pass, how much it removed, and what stopped it removing anything.
logsLog searchThe log view failing to answer a search.
databaseDatabaseThe database migration: what it migrated, what it refused, and what it left damaged.
adminAdministrationThe administrator account: a password changed or not changed, a user added or removed, a new signing secret, the administration interface's own connection — joined, ended, or presenting a session token this server did not issue — and a request from the administrator whose body the server could not read.
mcpAssistant surfaceThe Model Context Protocol endpoint, when it is enabled: a caller it would not let in, named by the address the request came from; a capability refusing a caller; a capability that changed the deployment; and the endpoint's own transport trouble. It files no entry for a read an assistant was entitled to, and no entry ever carries a credential.
callsCallsA call an operator acted on, such as pinning one. The current server writes nothing under this name; on a database upgraded from the previous server it holds the entries that server wrote.
legacyFrom the previous serverEntries that arrived before this field existed, or from a server that does not write it.

Entries written by the previous server were not rewritten. They were filed under the subsystem their old prefix names — invalid login attempt became a login entry, dirwatch.walkdir: a dirwatch entry — and anything that matches no prefix is shown as From the previous server. A log you had before the upgrade is still readable, and still filterable.

Searching

The log view has six controls and two buttons.

The log view's controls
ControlWhat it does
Sort orderOldest first or newest first. Newest first is the default, and is what you want when something just broke.
DateNarrows to one day, and the window depends on the sort order. Oldest first takes the minute you chose and runs forward a full day. Newest first runs back a day from the minute you chose and then back again by that same hour and minute, so the window is shorter than a day and usually lands on the day before the one you typed. An empty table after choosing today is normally this, not a log with nothing in it: try the other sort order, or the same date at 00:00.
LevelInformative, Warning, or Error, or all of them.
SubsystemOne of the names above, or all of them.
TextA substring of the message, matched without regard to case. A % or an _ you type matches itself.
Auto-refreshKeeps the view current, once every ten seconds, and skips a refresh while one is already in flight.
ReloadRuns the search again.
ResetClears every filter and runs the search again.

Above the table is a strip of counts: how many entries each part of the server wrote among everything your filters match, noisiest first. They are buttons. Clicking Directory watchers (137) sets the subsystem filter to dirwatch and gives you a log that is only those 137 entries. The counts deliberately ignore the subsystem filter you already set — a strip narrowed to the one subsystem you chose would offer nothing to narrow to next — so they always add up to the total of the search you are looking at.

Entries are paged: the view shows ten at a time and asks the server for two hundred at a time.

Retention

The Prune days option is how long the call history and the log are kept, and the server applies it once an hour. 0 switches the retention off, and a deployment with the retention off writes no retention entry at all. A pass that ran says what it removed: 

info prune: the retention pass removed 1204 calls and 318 log entries

A pass that could not run says that instead, and says why. A pass that wrote its notice before it started made a failed pass look exactly like a successful one, and a pass that had stopped removing anything was invisible until the disk was full.

Reading the log when something is wrong

Where to look, by what you are chasing
What you are chasingStart here
Recordings are not being picked upDirectory watchers, then Call ingest. A watch that started names the directory; a watch that stopped, or a directory that could not be read, names the directory and the failure; a recording that matches no talkgroup says so.
A call was recorded but never reached another instanceDownstreams — the line names the system, the talkgroup, the destination, and the outcome.
Calls are being held and not releasedDelayed calls.
Someone cannot sign in, or something is tryingLogins. Attempts, refusals, and the address they came from. A sign-in that worked writes nothing here; Administration is where the interface's connection appears.
Clients cannot listenAccess codes and Live feed.
Audio will not playAudio conversion. The entry carries what the converter said, and the reason is at the end of it.
A capture box's upload is refusedUploads. The entry names the reason the server gave, which is the text the box gets back.
The server restarted, or stoppedServer.
A system, talkgroup, or unit appeared on its ownConfiguration. Each entry names the recording that caused the server to create it, so the question becomes which recording that was.
The administration interface itself is doing something oddAdministration. The connection joining and ending, a session token this server did not issue, a new signing secret — which ends every session that was open before it — and a save whose body the server could not read.
You are not sure the history is being trimmedRetention. A pass that ran says how much it removed; a pass that could not run says what stopped it.
You are not sure the log itself is workingLog search — the log view's own failures are entries too.
An upgrade from the previous server went wrongDatabase: what it migrated, what it refused, and what it left damaged.

A text search is how you narrow inside a subsystem: Call ingest plus the talkgroup number, Directory watchers plus the directory, Logins plus the address.

15 · Tools

The Tools section is where a deployment moves in and out of files: the configuration out as one JSON file, a configuration back in, a talkgroup or unit list from another application, and the administrator password.

Export and import the configuration

Export config downloads the saved configuration as one JSON file: every section as the server has it, with the working copies of open sections left out. It is the deployment's own record — the file you keep before an upgrade, the file you copy to a second deployment, and the file you attach when you ask for help.

Import loads a configuration JSON file into the sections' working copies. It does not write anything: the caption under the picker says it plainly, because the difference matters. After an import, each section holds unsaved changes and its save bar is enabled, and the deployment changes only when you save the sections you want to apply.

An import is a whole configuration arriving in a running deployment. Save the sections you checked, and discard the ones you did not: the sections you leave alone keep their unsaved import in the working copy, and a save bar pressed later writes them. Importing a configuration from another deployment brings its access codes, its API keys, and its downstreams with it.

Import talkgroups and units from CSV

A talkgroup list from another application is imported per system. Pick the system, choose the CSV file, and the section shows you the rows it is about to write before you import them.

The CSV imports
ImportColumnsNotes
Import talkgroupsid, frequency, label, group, name, tag, descriptionGroups and tags the file names that the deployment does not have are created automatically. The rows are written into the system you picked.
Import unitsid, labelThe units are written into the system you picked.

The preview table lists the rows with a remove control on each, so a file that carries rows you do not want is edited on the way in, not after.

Change the password

The password panel takes the current password, a new one, and the new one again to verify it. The new password is at least eight characters, and the server checks the current password before it writes anything: a change with the wrong current password is refused, and the log says the password was not changed and why.

A server still running the password it shipped with says so in the todos banner at the top of the administration interface, and the banner is quiet once the password is changed. Changing the password does not end the sessions that are open: the session token is signed with the server's signing secret, not with the password. See security hardening.

A password you have lost is recovered with the program itself, not with the interface: the -admin_password flag stores a new administrator password on the machine where the server runs, where the database is. The password you type is a command-line argument, so it is visible to the other processes on that machine — run it where the server runs, and not in front of a share.

16 · The HTTP REST API

The server answers HTTP for three kinds of caller: an administrator session, a listener presenting an access code, and an ingest source presenting an API key. Everything the administration interface does, it does through these endpoints, so what you can do from a screen you can do from a script.

The three credentials

How each credential is presented
CredentialWhere it goesWhat it opens
Administrator sessionThe Authorization header, carrying the token from the login endpoint with no Bearer prefixEvery administration endpoint: the configuration, the log, the alerts, the password, the access users
Access codeThe X-Access-Code headerThe call history endpoints only, beside an administrator session. A server with no access list answers them to an anonymous caller.
API keyThe key field of an upload's multipart bodyThe two upload endpoints

The session token is signed with the server's signing secret and is valid for seven days: the server keeps the last five tokens it issued, and a server that generates a new secret ends every session opened before it. A refused request is answered 401 with an empty body, on every entry point, so a script never learns which credential it was missing.

The endpoint list

The OpenAPI section of the administration interface renders this list from the contract the server publishes, grouped the way the contract groups it, with the credential each endpoint takes. The list below is the same list, with what each endpoint is for.

The endpoints the server answers
Method and pathTakesWhat it does
POST /api/admin/loginnothingExchanges the administrator password for a session token, and reports that the shipped password is still in use.
POST /api/admin/logoutsessionInvalidates the token the caller presents.
GET /api/admin/configsessionThe whole configuration, under the key config.
PUT /api/admin/configsessionReplaces configuration sections from a whole-configuration body. Only the top-level keys the body names are applied.
GET /api/admin/config/{section}sessionOne section.
PUT /api/admin/config/{section}sessionReplaces one section, persists it, and broadcasts the whole configuration to the administration sessions that are open.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/sitessessionThe sites of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/sitessessionSaves the sites of one system.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/talkgroupssessionThe talkgroups of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/talkgroupssessionSaves the talkgroups of one system, and the system's blacklist with them when the body carries it.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/unitssessionThe units of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/unitssessionSaves the units of one system.
GET /api/admin/alertssessionThe named alert oscillator sequences the alert selects list.
POST /api/admin/logssessionSearches the log: sort order, date, level, subsystem, text, and paging.
GET /api/admin/statussessionReads what the server is doing right now: uptime, open connections, the watchers actually running, the calls waiting out a hold, the last 24 hours of calls, and the errors and warnings the log holds. The dashboard is built from this read.
POST /api/admin/passwordsessionChanges the administrator password. The current password is verified.
POST /api/admin/user-addsessionAdds a listener access code, with its ident, expiration, limit, and scope.
POST /api/admin/user-removesessionRemoves every access code sharing the user name the body names.
POST /api/calls/searchsession or access codeSearches the recorded calls, inside the caller's scope.
GET /api/calls/{callId}session or access codeOne recorded call.
GET /api/calls/{callId}/audiosession or access codeOne recording.
POST /api/call-uploadthe key fieldUploads a call as multipart form fields.
POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-uploadthe key fieldDeprecated. Uploads a trunk-recorder call: the JSON sidecar in meta, the recording in audio. A future release removes it; post the same call to /api/call-upload as form fields.
GET /nothingThe scanner webapp.
GET /adminnothingRedirects to /admin/, so the interface's relative addresses resolve inside its own subtree.
GET /admin/nothingThe administration interface.

Two connections, not requests

Two paths take a connection rather than a request.

  • The listener connection is taken over the address the scanner webapp is served from: the same path answers a browser and a listener, and the upgrade header decides which. The server asks a restricted server's listeners for an access code, sends the configuration their scope grants, and streams the calls. This connection is reserved for Saubeo Solutions and its native applications; the position is stated in chapter 27.
  • The administration connection at /api/admin/config is how an open administration session learns that the configuration changed: a save on the server is broadcast to every session, which is what makes the conflict banner appear on a page that is already open.

What the endpoints answer

  • Administration endpoints answer JSON, and a failure is answered with the status and an empty body.
  • The upload endpoints answer plain text, because the recorders that post to them read a line, not a JSON document: Call imported successfully. when the call was taken, Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>. with 401 when the credential refused it. See the upload endpoints.
  • A method an endpoint does not take is answered 405; the upload endpoints answer it with a line of text, and file it in the log, because a recorder posting with the wrong method is a standing misconfiguration.

The endpoints that write are the endpoints the interface uses, and they write to the running server: a configuration written through the API takes effect at once, is broadcast to the open administration sessions, and is filed in the log as a configuration change. The flags are not in this list — the flags chapter is where those are set.

Reading the contract

The contract the server publishes is machine-readable and is what the OpenAPI section reads. It names each path, its method, the credential it takes, and the shape of the bodies. The section is the quickest way to see what a running server answers, and it is the source the endpoint table above is checked against.

17 · The MCP server

The server can answer the Model Context Protocol: an assistant connected to your deployment can read the configuration, search the calls and the log, and — when it presents the administrator's credential — change the deployment. It is off by default, and it is mounted at /mcp.

Enabling it

The endpoint exists only when the server is started with -mcp_server, and the ini file carries the same setting as mcp_server = true. With the flag off, the path is not registered: the server answers nothing there, and the surface leaves no trace in the log.

Who reaches it, and how far

The endpoint has no credential of its own. It reads the same two credentials the rest of the server reads, and the credential decides the tier.

The two tiers, and what each one may do
Credential presentedTierWhat it opens
Authorization with an administrator session tokenAdministratorRead and write: the whole endpoint
X-Access-Code with a listener access codeRead-onlyThe call history and the configuration reads, inside the scope that code carries
Nothing, on a server with no access listRead-onlyThe reads the anonymous listener is entitled to
Anything the server does not acceptrefusedAn empty 401, and the protocol handler is never reached

The administrator's credential is examined first, so a stale access-code header on an administrator's request cannot get the administrator refused as a listener. A refusal is filed under the Assistant surface subsystem naming the address the request came from — what the caller presented is a credential, and a credential is not written in the log.

What the endpoint carries

The capabilities are the server's own use cases, reached through the same handlers the administration interface uses. The surface adds no capability of its own, and no path from it reaches a listener connection.

The tools
ToolReachWhat it does
list_systemsRead-only and administratorThe systems, as the configuration has them.
search_callsRead-only and administratorSearches the recorded calls, inside the caller's scope.
get_callRead-only and administratorOne call, with its recording.
diagnose_feed_problemRead-only and administratorOne pass over the calls, the log, and the configuration for a listener who hears nothing.
inspect_systemAdministratorA system with its sites, talkgroups, units, alerts, and colours.
search_logsAdministratorThe log, with the filters the log view has.
explain_errorAdministratorOne log entry, read against the configuration that produced it.
analyze_healthAdministratorThe deployment's state: the log's warnings and errors, the configuration, the retention.
manage_configAdministrator, writesReads and replaces a configuration section, and a system's sites, talkgroups, and units.
manage_access_userAdministrator, writesAdds and removes listener access codes.
rotate_admin_passwordAdministrator, writesChanges the administrator password.
The prompts
PromptWhat it asks an assistant to do
daily_health_reviewRead a day of the deployment: the log's warnings and errors, the configuration, and what changed.
explain_recent_errorsTake the recent log errors and say what they have in common.
troubleshoot_silent_talkgroupFind out why a talkgroup stopped reporting.
audit_access_codesRead the access codes: who is expiring, who is at its limit, who has no scope.
onboard_listenerWrite an access code for a listener: ident, scope, expiry.

The resources are the configuration read as documents: the version, the systems, the options, the groups, the tags, the access codes, the API keys, the watched directories, the downstreams, the alerts, a system's sites, talkgroups, and units, and a slice of the log by level and date. The listener-facing ones are open to the read-only tier; the rest are the administrator's.

An assistant holding an administrator session token can change the deployment: it can add an access code, replace a section, and change the administrator password. Treat that token as the credential it is — give it to the assistant that needs it, for the session that needs it, and end it when the work is done. Every change a tool makes is filed in the log, so the log is where you see what the assistant did.

18 · The command line client

The program you installed is also a client of a server that is already running. Run it with -cmd and an action, and it logs in, does the thing, and stops — the same administration endpoints the interface uses, from a shell, in a script, on a machine that has no browser open.

It talks to a server over its address, so it needs no database and no configuration of the deployment: it is a client, and it can be run anywhere that can reach the server.

The actions

The -cmd actions
ActionWhat it doesOptions it takes
loginSigns in and keeps the session token for the commands that follow+password, or the environment
logoutEnds the session the token file holdsnone
config-getWrites the server's configuration to a file+out <file.json>
config-setSends a configuration file to the server, applying the sections it names+in <file.json>
admin-passwordGives the server a new administrator password+password <password>
user-addAdds a listener access code+ident, +code, and the optional +expiration, +limit, +systems
user-removeRemoves every access code sharing an ident+ident <ident>
helpPrints the list above, with the examples and the defaults for your systemnone
The options every action takes
OptionWhat it names
+urlThe server to talk to. Default http://localhost:3000/. An address that is not http or https stops the client before it reads anything else.
+tokenThe session token keystore. Default is a file named for the program, in the folder the server writes its data in.
+systemsThe systems an access code is scoped to, as system identifiers: 10001,10002.
+expirationAn access code's expiry, in RFC 3339 form.
+limitAn access code's simultaneous-listener cap.

Logging in without leaving the password in the shell

The client reads the password from the environment first, which is why the usage text shows the login this way: 

$ RDIO_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<password> ./rdio-scanner -cmd login
$ ./rdio-scanner -cmd config-get +out deployment.json
$ ./rdio-scanner -cmd user-add +ident "Dispatch desk" +code 7F2K9Q +systems 10001 +expiration 2026-12-31T00:00:00Z

+password <password> works the same and is what you use on Windows, where the shell makes the environment form awkward. A password typed as an argument is visible to every other process on the machine, so on a machine you share, use the environment.

The session lives in the token file, so a script logs in once and runs its commands, and a command run with no session says Not logged in. and stops. A command that could not be done is reported with the failure and ends with a non-zero status, which is what a script needs: a command run against a server that is not answering is told it did not happen.

The flags the client mode is not

Three flags are the program doing the work itself, on the machine where it runs, with no server involved:

The flags that act on the deployment, not on a running server
FlagWhat it does
-admin_password <password>Stores a new administrator password in the deployment's database, says so in the log, and stops without starting a server. This is the way back from a lost password.
-config_saveWrites the configuration the flags named into the ini file, and stops. See the flags chapter.
-versionPrints the version and stops.

config-set writes the sections a file names, and only those. A file exported from another deployment carries its access codes, its API keys, and its downstreams, and sending it changes who can listen to this deployment and where its calls go.

19 · TLS and HTTPS

The server answers https by itself, in two ways: with a certificate you provide, or with one it obtains from Let's Encrypt. Both are flags, both are saved in the ini file, and both name the address the https listener answers on.

Your own certificate

Point the server at a PEM-formatted certificate and its key, and name the address to answer on: 

./rdio-scanner -listen :80 -ssl_listen :443 \
    -ssl_cert_file mycert.crt -ssl_key_file mykey.key

The certificate and the key belong together: the server starts the https listener only when both are named, and a key that does not match the certificate is one of the ways this chapter's failure looks. When your certificate comes from an authority that signs it with an intermediate certificate, append the intermediate's contents to the certificate file, in the order the authority gave them to you. The server reads one file, not two.

A certificate from Let's Encrypt

Name a domain and the server takes care of the certificate, the key, and the renewal: 

./rdio-scanner -listen :80 -ssl_listen :443 -ssl_auto_cert radio.example.org
  • The domain must point at this machine. The authority verifies the name by reaching back to it, so an address record that points elsewhere, or a machine behind a router that does not forward the port, fails the request.
  • The https port must be reachable from the internet. The certificate is obtained over that port. The project's guidance is to have 80 and 443 both open, and the domain pointing at the server.
  • One domain per server. The name you give is the only name the server will obtain a certificate for; a second host name on the same deployment is refused by the server's own policy.
  • The certificates live in the base directory, in an autocert folder beside the database. Keep them: they are the deployment's credentials, and a base directory that is thrown away on upgrade throws the certificate away with it, to be obtained again.

The server accepts the authority's terms of service on your behalf, which is what makes the whole exchange automatic: no request, no renewal, no restart.

The address the https listener answers on

-ssl_listen takes an address and a port, the same form as -listen. Name it with a port. A server configured with -ssl_listen and no port has always answered on 3000, not 443, and this server keeps that behavior rather than moving existing deployments: -ssl_listen :443 is what you type.

Ports below 1024 need root privileges on Linux, macOS, and FreeBSD. Run the server as root, give the container the capability to bind them, or answer on a high port and put a proxy in front of it — chapter 20.

Both addresses answer

Starting a server with TLS does not shut the plain address down: it answers http and https at the same time, and the console says so: 

Rdio Scanner v8.0.0
----------------------------------
server started
main interface at http://radio.example.org
main interface at https://radio.example.org
admin interface at https://radio.example.org/admin

There is no redirect from http to https. A deployment that must answer only https says so at the boundary: bind the plain address to the machine itself with -listen 127.0.0.1:3000 and let the proxy terminate TLS, or answer http on a port you do not open in the firewall.

When the https listener cannot start

A server that asked for https and cannot answer it does not carry on as a plain http server. The failure is written to the log under the Server subsystem, said on the console beside it, and the server shuts down the way it shuts down for an interrupt: the plain address stops with it, and the database closes.

The causes are the usual ones, and the log line names the address it could not answer:

What stops an https listener, and what it says
CauseWhat you see
The certificate file is missing, unreadable, or not PEMThe server stops at startup, and the log's Server entry carries the reason the listener gave.
The key does not match the certificateSame: the server stops, and the reason is in the log entry.
The port is already takenThe server stops. Find the process holding the port, or name a different one.
The authority cannot reach the domainThe listener starts and the certificate request fails. The failure appears on the console as a TLS error, and the browser is served a certificate the authority did not issue.

TLS handshake failures and other HTTP server complaints go to the console, not to the log view: the server hands its listeners a writer, not a logger, so a deployment running under a service manager finds them in the manager's own record — journalctl, the Windows event log.

This server does not create a certificate. The flag that generated a self-signed certificate is gone, and a deployment that names it is told the flag is not recognized. Use your own certificate, Let's Encrypt, or a proxy that terminates TLS.

20 · Reverse proxies and trusted proxies

A deployment that answers on the standard ports, shares a machine with other sites, or needs a certificate a proxy holds, runs behind a proxy. Two things must survive the proxy: the connection a listener holds open, and the address the server is supposed to believe.

nginx

The configuration below is the one the project carries as its nginx example, with the site's own root left in place. The server is reached as an upstream on its own port, and the location that carries it strips the site's prefix off the address before forwarding. 

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

upstream rdio-scanner {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
}

server {
    listen 80 default_server;
    listen [::]:80 default_server;

    # listen 443 ssl default_server;
    # ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/certs/site.pem;
    # ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/site.key;

    server_name _;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }

    location /rdio-scanner/ {
        rewrite ^/rdio-scanner/(.*)$ /$1 break;
        proxy_pass http://rdio-scanner;
    }

    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
}

The four lines at the bottom of the server block are the whole of it. HTTP/1.1, the Upgrade header, and a Connection header that says upgrade when the client asked for an upgrade and close when it did not — that is what lets the listener connection through. A proxy that drops the upgrade answers the page and refuses the connection, and the webapp sits there with no calls.

Apache

Apache does the same job with mod_proxy, mod_proxy_http, and mod_proxy_wstunnel enabled. The project's Apache example is a stub: it says what it is for and leaves the file to you. This is the shape it is describing. 

LoadModule proxy_module modules/mod_proxy.so
LoadModule proxy_http_module modules/mod_proxy_http.so
LoadModule proxy_wstunnel_module modules/mod_proxy_wstunnel.so

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName radio.example.org

    ProxyPreserveHost On
    ProxyPass /rdio-scanner/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/
    ProxyPassReverse /rdio-scanner/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/

    RewriteEngine On
    RewriteCond %{HTTP:Upgrade} websocket [NC]
    RewriteCond %{HTTP:Connection} upgrade [NC]
    RewriteRule ^/rdio-scanner/(.*) ws://127.0.0.1:3000/$1 [P,L]
</VirtualHost>

ProxyPreserveHost On forwards the host name the browser asked for, which is what a deployment answering several names needs. The rewrite rule sends an upgrade request to the tunnel handler; without it, Apache forwards the upgrade as an ordinary request and the connection is not made.

What a proxy must not do

Proxy settings that break a deployment
SettingWhat it does to the deployment
Buffering left onThe proxy collects the audio and the call stream instead of passing them, and listeners hear calls arrive in blocks. Turn it off for the location: proxy_buffering off;, ProxyEnableForwarding-style buffering directives, whichever your proxy uses.
A short read timeoutA listener connection is open for as long as the listener is listening. The server bounds one request at 30 seconds and keeps keep-alives on; a proxy that closes an idle connection at 60 seconds drops every listener on the deployment once a minute. Set the read and send timeouts on that location to hours, not minutes.
The upgrade headers droppedThe page loads, the connection is refused, and nothing plays. The four proxy lines above are the requirement, not an optimization.
The host header rewrittenA deployment that answers several names, or a certificate obtained for one name, stops matching what the browser asked for. Forward the host as the browser sent it.

Proxying under a prefix

Both examples serve the deployment under /rdio-scanner/ and strip that prefix before forwarding, so the server sees the address it was written to answer. Two consequences are worth knowing before you point a listener at a proxied deployment:

  • The address a listener connects to is the proxied address, prefix included: wss://radio.example.org/rdio-scanner/. The upgrade header is what decides whether a request for that address is a page or a listener, and the proxy must pass it.
  • /admin answers a redirect that adds the trailing slash, so the administration interface's relative addresses resolve inside its own subtree. A proxy that rewrites the prefix must let that redirect through, and a client that follows it must keep the prefix.

Trusted proxies

Behind a proxy, every connection arrives from the proxy's address. That is a problem the server can only fix with your help, because the address the server is given is the machine that forwarded the request, and the server's limits are counted per address:

  • Three failed logins from one address lock that address out for ten minutes. Behind an unnamed proxy, one user's three guesses lock out everyone behind that proxy.
  • A listener's access attempts are capped per session and per address, and the log names the address the attempt came from.
  • Every log entry that names an address — a refused credential, a login, an ingest — names the machine that forwarded the request.

-trusted_proxies names the proxies whose forwarding header the server believes: a comma-separated list of addresses and CIDR prefixes, 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, ::1. When the connection arrives from one of them, the server reads the leftmost usable address out of X-Forwarded-For and uses that as the address of the client — so the lockout counts the machine that guessed, and the log names it. 

listen = :3000
trusted_proxies = 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8

A trusted proxy is a machine you are telling the server to believe, and the header it forwards is written by whoever is on the other side of it. Name the proxy's own address, and nothing broader: a prefix that covers the internet is a list of addresses whose logins, access attempts, and log entries the server will attribute to whoever types the header.

Embedding the listener interface in a page

The project carries a starter page that puts the listener interface in a frame beside your own text: an iframe sized for a phone, a stylesheet that keeps it centered and responsive, and room for the instructions your listeners need. It is a page you serve yourself, and the only setting in it is the address of the deployment. 

<iframe src="" width="410" height="608"></iframe>

Put the frame on the same host name the deployment answers on, so the browser treats the page and the interface as one site and the listener connection is not blocked as a third-party connection. Serve it over the same scheme as the deployment: a page on https asking for a deployment on http is refused by the browser before the connection is made.

The frame carries the listener interface. The administration interface is not for embedding: it is the machine room, and it is opened by the people who run it.

21 · Running as a service

A deployment you have to start by hand is a deployment that is down while you are asleep. The program installs and controls itself as a service on Linux, Windows, macOS, and FreeBSD, and the same five words do it on every one of them.

The service mode

The -service actions
ActionWhat it does
installRegisters the service with the operating system's service manager, and writes into the service's own configuration the command the manager runs it with.
uninstallRemoves the service from the manager. Your configuration, your database, and your recordings stay where they are.
start, stop, restartAsk the manager to do it. The command is a client of the manager: it asks, reports, and ends.
runThe action the manager starts the service with. It is written into the service configuration at install time; you do not type it.

Installing and controlling the service needs the privileges the manager asks for: root on Linux, macOS, and FreeBSD, an elevated command prompt on Windows. The service runs as the account that installed it, which is normally the system's most privileged account, so the deployment's folder must be a folder you are content for that account to write in.

The service is registered under the name rdio-scanner, and on FreeBSD under rdioscanner, because that manager does not accept a name with a hyphen in it. Its display name is Rdio Scanner and its description is The perfect software-defined radio companion, which is what you see in the manager's own tools.

Stopping the service is the same shutdown as pressing the keys in a terminal: the server is told to stop, closes its addresses, and closes the database. A control the manager refuses ends with a non-zero status and no explanation, which is what a script needs and all a script gets.

A service has no terminal, so the console lines the server prints — the addresses it answers on, the ffmpeg notice, the TLS failures — go to the manager's record, not to a window. The log view is where the deployment's own messages are, and chapter 14 is how to read it.

Linux

The archive for a Linux deployment is rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v<version>.zip, and the builds for 386, ARM, and ARM64 are the same archive with the target named in its place. The Linux builds carry their own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for the architecture they run on, so nothing has to be installed on the host for recordings to convert. 

$ mkdir rdio-scanner && cd rdio-scanner
$ unzip ~/Downloads/rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zip
$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service install
$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/rdio-scanner.service that runs the program with -service run. From then on the manager owns the process: 

$ sudo systemctl status rdio-scanner
$ sudo journalctl -u rdio-scanner -f
$ sudo systemctl restart rdio-scanner

The server's console lines are in the journal. The deployment's own record is in the log view, and a line you read in the journal that the log view does not carry is a line the server printed before it had a database to write to.

Open the port the deployment answers on. With ufw: 

$ sudo ufw allow 3000/tcp

A server answering on 80 and 443 needs those ports open, and a server answering them must be run by a privileged account, which a service installed as root is. A container that must answer them is given the capability to bind them, and chapter 4 is the container's own chapter.

Windows

The Windows archive is rdio-scanner-windows-amd64-v<version>.zip and carries the program as rdio-scanner.exe, with ffmpeg and ffprobe inside it. Run the install from a command prompt opened as Administrator, in the folder you extracted the archive into — the service is registered with the path it was installed from, and moving the folder afterwards leaves the service pointing at a program that is no longer there. 

C:\rdio-scanner> rdio-scanner.exe -service install
C:\rdio-scanner> rdio-scanner.exe -service start

The service appears in the Services console as Rdio Scanner, started manually by default: set its startup type to Automatic if you want it to come up with the machine. The manager's own tools work on it as they work on any service — sc query rdio-scanner, net start rdio-scanner, and the same two commands with stop.

Windows does not let a program answer the standard ports the way a privileged Unix account does, and its firewall asks once per program. Allow rdio-scanner.exe through Windows Defender Firewall on the private network the machine sits on, and open the port on the public network if listeners reach the deployment from outside: 

C:\rdio-scanner> netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Rdio Scanner" dir=in action=allow program="C:\rdio-scanner\rdio-scanner.exe" enable=yes

A Windows deployment that answers 80 and 443 behind a proxy is the arrangement chapter 20 describes; a deployment that answers them directly needs the certificate chapter 19 describes.

macOS

The macOS archive is rdio-scanner-macos-amd64-v<version>.zip for an Intel machine and rdio-scanner-macos-arm64-v<version>.zip for an Apple one. Both carry their own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio on a macOS machine for the architecture they run on, so nothing has to be installed on the host for recordings to convert. A macOS ffmpeg binary is compiled with macOS's own compiler and linker, so this build compiles them on the machine that is the target: go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg on that Mac compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts. The two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives — go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 compiles the Intel binaries there, and Rosetta 2 is what lets that Mac run them. The arm64 binaries compiled on an Intel Mac are run on an Apple Silicon Mac, because an Intel machine will not execute them: the compile leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory and names the Mac that runs them, and the operator carries them there. The machine that produces the releases runs neither program, which is why a release run there skips these targets and ships the five archives it can ship. The archive's FFMPEG.txt names the host that compiled them, the codecs the run recorded, and the command that built them there. 

% sudo ./rdio-scanner -service install
% sudo ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a launchd property list at /Library/LaunchDaemons/rdio-scanner.plist, and the daemon is registered with the name rdio-scanner. The manager's own commands work on it: 

% sudo launchctl list | grep rdio
% sudo launchctl stop rdio-scanner

macOS asks you to allow the program when it first accepts incoming connections; answer Allow, and answer it again when the program is replaced by a new version, because the allowance belongs to the program you allowed. A deployment behind a proxy on the same machine needs no allowance for the port the proxy connects to.

FreeBSD

The FreeBSD archive is rdio-scanner-freebsd-amd64-v<version>.zip. The FreeBSD build carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio on a FreeBSD machine, so nothing has to be installed on the host for recordings to convert. FreeBSD is compiled on FreeBSD, so this build compiles it on the machine that is the target — go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg on that box, running gmake because ffmpeg's build asks for GNU make and FreeBSD's base make is not it — and the archive's FFMPEG.txt names the host that compiled them, the codecs the run recorded, and the command that built them there. 

# ./rdio-scanner -service install
# ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a service script at /usr/local/etc/rc.d/rdioscanner, and the service is known to the system as rdioscanner — the hyphenated name is what that manager rejects, which is why FreeBSD is the one system whose service is spelled differently. 

# service rdioscanner status
# service rdioscanner restart

Open the port in the packet filter. With pf, a rule passing the deployment's port on the external interface, reloaded, is the whole firewall step; a deployment behind a proxy on the same host needs the rule only for the address the proxy answers on.

What the service changes about the deployment

  • The base directory is the folder the installed path lives in. The configuration, the database, the recordings, and the migration archive are written there. A folder on a mount that is not mounted at boot is a deployment that starts with a new database beside the one you meant it to open.
  • The service starts before you are logged in, and as the account that installed it. A deployment whose base directory is inside a user's home folder is a deployment a privileged account writes into that home. Give the deployment a folder of its own.
  • The timezone is the machine's. A server whose machine is set to the wrong zone writes a log and a call history in the wrong hours, and the log view's dates follow it. Set the machine's time zone, not the server's.
  • Updating the program is a stop, a replace, and a start. The service configuration points at the path, so replacing the file in place keeps the service working. Back up first — chapter 23 — and expect the first start to migrate the database, chapter 24.

22 · Security hardening

A deployment holds four things worth protecting: the administrator's credential, the secret that signs its sessions, the credentials that let audio in, and the credentials that let people listen. The server has one model for each, and the hardening is knowing what each one is, and what it costs to leave it as it shipped.

The credentials and what they are

The four credentials a deployment holds
CredentialWhat it opensWhere it lives
The administrator passwordEverything: the configuration, the log, the access codes, the ingest keys, the password itselfHashed with bcrypt in the database. The cost is -bcrypt_cost, 10 to 14, default 10.
The signing secretThe power to mint administrator sessionsIn the database's options. Generated on a start that found none; a secret found too short to be safe is replaced.
An ingest API keyOne path: posting a call to an upload endpointIn the configuration, listed in the API Keys section.
A listener access codeThe calls its scope covers, for as long as it is valid, up to its limitIn the configuration, listed in the Access section.

The session token is not a credential you store: it is a signature the server makes with its secret, valid for seven days, and the server keeps the last five it issued. Signing in ends the sessions older than the five, and a server that changes its secret ends every session opened before the change — which is why the console says it out loud on the start that does it, and why restoring a database from a backup ends the sessions opened on the deployment you restored over.

The checklist

Hardening, in the order it pays
Do thisBecauseChapter
Change the administrator password on the first dayThe shipped password is published, and the interface tells you that you are still using it in the todos banner.15
Raise the bcrypt cost to 12 or more on a machine that can afford the millisecondsThe cost is the price of guessing the password offline. It applies to the next password you store, not to the one already stored.6
Answer over TLS, directly or through a proxyThe login sends a password, and the session token is the credential itself after that. On a network you do not own, plain http hands both to anyone listening.19, 20
Name your proxy in -trusted_proxiesBehind an unnamed proxy, every login arrives from the proxy's address, and the login lockout counts per address: one user's three guesses lock out everyone behind that proxy.20
Give every access code a scope, an expiry, and a limitAn access code with no scope is every call on the deployment. An access code with no expiry is a credential you cannot stop handing out.9
Set the retention daysA deployment that keeps every call and every log entry forever keeps a recording of every transmission it has ever heard, on a disk that fills.13, 14
Keep the base directory readable by the deployment's account and by nobody who mattersThe ini file, the database, the recordings, and the autocert cache are all in it. The database holds the password hash, the secret, the ingest keys, and the access codes.5
Do not put credentials in a command line you type on a shared machineA command-line argument is visible to every other process on the machine. The client reads the password from the environment first for this reason.18
Treat an administrator session token as a credential when you hand it to an assistantThe assistant surface writes when it presents that token: it can add an access code, replace a section, change the password.17
Back up the base directory before you update, and before you migrateThe migration rewrites the database in place.23, 24

The limits the server already runs

What the server refuses, and how
LimitValueWhat it looks like from outside
Administrator logins per addressThree in a ten-minute windowThe address is refused for the rest of the window. The answer is an empty 401, with no hint of how many attempts are left. The lockout is one warning in the log, under Logins, per window.
Access attemptsFive per session, and five per addressA listener who has used the five is refused, and a listener whose fifth attempt arrives while they are locked out is refused as locked out — a valid code included.
Simultaneous listenersMaxClients, default 200, and per access codeThe connection is refused in silence: the server does not tell the caller why.
Session tokens keptThe last five issuedA sixth login ends the oldest session.
Every refusal—An empty body and a status, on every entry point, so a script never learns which credential it was missing.

What the server does not do

Knowing the shape of the model is knowing where the work is yours:

  • One administrator. There is no second administrator account, no roles, no per-section permissions. Anyone with the password can do everything, so the password is the secret of the deployment, and the people who do not need it do not have it.
  • No second factor. The password is the credential. TLS, a proxy that is not reachable from the internet, and a password nobody guesses are the controls.
  • No address allowlist. The server answers whoever connects. Restricting who reaches the deployment is the firewall's and the proxy's job.
  • No rate limit on the upload endpoints. An ingest key is a key: anyone holding it posts calls. Rotate a key you think is loose, and watch the log under Uploads, where the refusals are filed, and Call ingest, where the calls it posts land.
  • No audit trail beyond the log. The log is the record: configuration changes, logins, refusals, lockouts, retention, migrations, the assistant surface's writes. It is filed by subsystem, and it is pruned by the retention setting — so a deployment that needs the record keeps the retention days long enough to hold it.

Nothing in the log is a credential. The server files addresses, subsystems, and outcomes, and never a password, a token, an ingest key, or an access code. That is what makes the log view safe to read aloud on a support call, and safe to keep.

23 · Backup and restore

A deployment is a program and a folder. The program is in the release archive and can be downloaded again; the folder cannot. Back up the folder, and the deployment is backed up.

What is in the folder

The files a deployment writes in its base directory
FileWhat it holdsBack it up
rdio-scanner.dbEverything the deployment knows: the systems, sites, talkgroups, units, groups, tags, options, access codes, ingest keys, downstreams, watched directories, the log, and the recordings themselves — each call's audio is stored in the call's row.Yes. This is the deployment.
rdio-scanner.iniThe flags you saved: the listening address, the database settings, TLS, trusted proxies, the bcrypt cost, the assistant surface.Yes. It is small, and it is the part you typed.
autocert/The certificates obtained from Let's Encrypt and their keys.Yes, or be ready to obtain them again.
The token file the client writesThe session token -cmd logs in with.Not worth backing up. It is a live credential, and it is re-made by logging in.
The program, and the ffmpeg it carriesThe code, and the converters compiled for its target.No. The release archive has them.

The recordings are in the database, which is the fact that makes a backup of a deployment one file rather than a tree: a call's audio travels with the call, so a database restored on a new machine plays its whole history, and a database restored without its recordings is a history of calls that play nothing.

Backing up

On the deployment's own database file, stop the server first. The server keeps the database open, and a file copied while a program is writing it is a file that may not be a database. 

$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service stop
$ cp rdio-scanner.db /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).db
$ cp rdio-scanner.ini /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).ini

On a server database, use the database's own tool, and the same settings the server uses: 

$ mysqldump --single-transaction -h 10.0.0.5 -u rdio -p rdio_scanner > /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).sql
$ pg_dump -h 10.0.0.5 -U rdio rdio_scanner > /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).sql

Back it up before you update, before you migrate, and before a retention change that will delete history. A deployment that records continuously is a deployment whose newest hour is the part a crash takes; a deployment that keeps a week of calls is a deployment whose history is worth a nightly copy.

The Tools section's export writes the configuration as one JSON file. It is a record of the configuration — the sections as the server has them — and it is not a backup: it carries no calls, no recordings, no log. It is what you send a second deployment, and what you attach when you ask for help. Chapter 15 is the section's own chapter.

Restoring

  1. Install the program you are restoring to, in the folder the deployment will live in, and put the ini file there. A deployment restored with the flags it was running with is the same deployment; a deployment restored with defaults answers on 3000 with a SQLite database in a folder you did not mean.
  2. Put the database where the configuration points. The same name, the same path, the same dialect. A SQLite file named rdio-scanner.db in the base directory is the default; a server database is loaded with the database's own tool, into the name the ini file names.
  3. Start the server. It applies the schema to the database it finds, which on a restored database is a pass that finds nothing to change, and says so in the log under Database.
  4. Expect every administrator session to be ended. The signing secret is in the database you restored, and it is not the secret the deployment you restored over was signing with. Log in again; the interface tells you the sessions it ended.

Then check the deployment as a listener: a call from the restored history plays, the systems are the ones you had, the access codes are the ones you issued, and the watched directories are watching the folders they were watching.

A backup you have never restored is a file you hope is a backup. Restore one onto a second machine, or onto a folder beside the deployment with a different -db_file, and start the server on it. The restore is the test, and it takes minutes.

24 · Upgrading and migrating

Updating the program is four steps. Migrating an older database is the first start of the new program doing it for you, announcing itself in the log, and archiving what it cannot carry instead of throwing it away.

Back up the base directory before you update. The migration rewrites the database in place, on the first start, with no second copy and no undo. Chapter 23 is the backup, and it takes a minute.

The update

  1. Stop the server. A database the server has open is a database you are about to rewrite.
  2. Back up the database and the ini file.
  3. Replace the program with the new release, in the same folder. The service is registered with the path, so replacing the file in place keeps the service working; a folder moved is a service pointing at a program that is no longer there.
  4. Start the server, and read what it says on the console and in the log.

The first start of a new server on a database it has already migrated changes nothing: every step of the pass probes what it is about to do, finds it done, and says nothing. The pass is safe to run twice, which is what makes a start after a failed start an ordinary start.

What the first start does to a version 6 database

The migration pass applies the new schema, repairs four things the new server needs that the old database does not have, and then moves the thirteen tables, in the order that order requires: groups, tags, systems, talkgroups, units, options, meta, logs, downstreams, watched directories, calls, ingest keys, access codes. The order is load-bearing: the talkgroup, unit, dirwatch, and call migrations resolve their references against the tables the earlier migrations have already filled, and the same pass run in another order migrates a different database.

The four repairs, and why each one is needed
RepairWhat it gives the database
The log's subsystem columnThe column naming the part of the server that wrote each entry, and the indexes the log search is written against. The entries the old server wrote are filed by what their text says.
The call's recording lengthThe column saying how long each recording lasts. Rows the migration cannot measure are left as never measured, and are filled when the call is played.
The migration archiveThe table left-behind rows are written into, so dropping an old table never destroys a row quietly.
The options key ruleThe duplicates an old MySQL deployment's saves left behind are removed, and the index that refuses duplicates is created over the deduplicated table.

Each old table the pass finds is announced in the log under Database — migrating groups... and its twelve siblings — and a database the new server created itself, or a version 7 database already migrated, is left exactly as it was, with nothing said.

A row the pass cannot carry does not stop the pass: the row is archived, the reason is written with it, and the migration continues. An old table is dropped only once every row in it has been carried or archived, so a table that survived because one row of it could not be read is read again on the next start, and its already-archived rows archive as nothing.

One class of rows the old server lost is carried by this one. The old migration wrote some of its text into its statements by escaping quotes and left the system blacklist, the system and talkgroup colours, the log level, the watched directory type, and the call audio type unescaped, so a single quote in one of those columns made its insert a syntax error and the row was lost. Those rows migrate here, as bound parameters.

The migration archive

The archive is a table in the deployment's database, named migrationArchive. Each row is one row the pass read and could not carry: the table it came from, its identifier there, the reason, its contents as JSON, and the moment it was archived. 

SELECT "tableName", "rowId", "reason", "archivedAt", "contents"
  FROM "migrationArchive"
 ORDER BY "tableName", "rowId";

Read it after the first start. A deployment whose archive is empty migrated completely; a deployment with rows in it has history the new schema does not hold, and the reason column says why — a reference that resolved to nothing, a row the old server had left damaged. What you do with them is your decision: re-enter the configuration the archive names, or leave the row as a record.

From the version 5 program

The version 5 server was a different program, and there is no upgrade path from it: the version 6 server replaced it. What carries over is the database, and the way to move it is a copy.

  1. Stop the version 5 server.
  2. Copy its database.sqlite into the folder the new program lives in, and rename the copy to rdio-scanner.db, the name the new server opens by default.
  3. Start the new program. It migrates the copy: the version 6 tables it finds are moved by the pass above, and the version 5 rows the version 6 server had already moved are simply the version 6 tables the pass reads.
  4. On MySQL or MariaDB, do not copy a file. Back the database up, and start the new program pointed at the same database with the -db_* flags — host, port, name, user, password, and -db_type naming the dialect. The pass runs against it in place.

The version 5 program is the Node-era program, and going back to it means restoring the database from before the copy and running the release you came from. That is the reason the copy is a copy: the migration writes into the file you gave it.

After the first start

  • Every administrator session is ended. The start that migrates is a start that checked the signing secret, and a secret made or replaced ends the sessions signed with the old one. Log in again.
  • Read the log under Database. The migration's notices, the rows it archived, and the units the old server left damaged are all there, filed by the pass that made them. Chapter 14 is how to filter to one subsystem.
  • Check the todos banner. A migration that carried your configuration clears the banner it had; a banner that names something missing after a migration is a configuration the archive holds, not a bug in the banner.
  • Play a call from before the update. It is the shortest test of the recordings, the talkgroup references, and the audio converter the new build carries.

Two servers on one database is not an update in progress. The migration is a pass that drops old tables when it is done, and a second server starting on the same database while it runs is a server reading tables that are being moved. Stop the old server before the new one starts, and on a container, the volume is the folder: one deployment, one volume.

25 · Troubleshooting

Start from what you see, not from what you suspect. Every symptom below has a place to look first, a log subsystem that names it, and a control that fixes it.

Symptom to place
You seeLook here firstChapter
A talkgroup that used to report is silentThe log, filtered to the subsystem that receives the audio, over the day it went quiet14
Calls arrive and play nothingThe conversion mode, and whether this build carries the converter13, 3
The login is refusedThe log under Logins, and the ten-minute window8, 22
A recorder's upload is refusedThe line the server answered, and the log under Uploads10
The webapp connects and hears nothingThe proxy's upgrade headers, the access code, the listener cap20, 9
A downstream deployment gets nothingThe log under Downstreams, and the answer the other server gave10
The log is full of one messageThe subsystem filter, and the count strip14
The build compiled macOS binaries that do not run on the Mac it compiled them onThe run is the binaries' own execution: the compile leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory and names the Mac that runs them, and the operator carries them there4, 21
The save bar will not save, or the conflict banner is upWhat the banner says, and the other session that saved8

A talkgroup that used to report is silent

  1. Open the log, filtered to the receiving subsystem, on the day it went quiet. A watched directory that stopped finding files says so; a recorder posting to the upload endpoints says so when its key stops working. The subsystem filter is the control that makes this one question, not a scroll.
  2. Is the recorder still writing? A recorder that stopped writing writes nothing to the server, and the server cannot report a file that never arrived. Look at the recorder's own output.
  3. Did the identifiers change? A watched directory names a talkgroup by the identifiers in the file name, resolved against the system. A recorder that changes its talkgroup numbering creates talkgroups you did not ask for when auto populate is on, and drops calls when it is off. The log names the system and talkgroup each call resolved to.
  4. Is the talkgroup in your scope? An access code scoped to some systems shows you those systems. Silence on a talkgroup you cannot see is a scope, not a fault.
  5. Is the call delayed? A system delay or a talkgroup delay holds a call out of the live stream for that long. It arrives in the history, and it arrives late.

Calls arrive and play nothing

  • The conversion mode. The four modes decide what the server does to an incoming recording. A mode that converts with ffmpeg needs ffmpeg: every release build carries it inside the program, compiled for audio, the five Linux and Windows ffmpeg binaries compiled by this project's build in a container, and the macOS and FreeBSD ffmpeg binaries compiled by this build on the machines that are their targets, with the one command chapter 4 lists. A program built with plain go build carries none. A deployment whose converter is missing says so on the console at startup, and the notice is worth reading on every new release.
  • The format the recorder writes. The server converts what it can; a recorder writing a format the converter refuses produces a call with a row and no playable audio. Play one on the server's own interface before you chase the network.
  • The recording length. Rows migrated from an older database carry no measured length, and a call whose length was never measured is a call the interface shows without a duration. The recording plays; the number is what is missing.

The login is refused

  • Three guesses in ten minutes lock the address out, and the refusal is an empty 401 that says nothing about the window. The log under Logins carries one warning per lockout, naming the address. Behind a proxy, the address is the proxy's — name the proxy in -trusted_proxies and the lockout counts the machine that guessed.
  • A token that stopped working is a secret that changed. The server keeps the last five tokens it issued, and a start that made or replaced the signing secret ends every session opened before it. The console says it, and the log files it.
  • A password you no longer have is changed with the program, on the machine, with -admin_password. It writes the credential into the deployment's database and stops without starting a server.

A recorder's upload is refused

The upload endpoints answer in plain text, and the line they answer with is the diagnosis:

The answers the upload endpoints give
The recorder was toldWhat it means
Call imported successfully.The call is in the database. If the listener does not show it, the problem is downstream of the ingest: scope, delay, or the connection.
Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>. with 401The key is not in the configuration, or it is scoped to a system and talkgroup the posting does not match. The API Keys section is where the key and its scope are.
A line of text answering 405The recorder posted with a method the endpoint does not take. The log files it, because a recorder doing it is a standing misconfiguration.

A call that arrives and vanishes is usually the duplicate window: two calls on the same system, talkgroup, and site within half a second are one call, and the second is dropped. A recorder posting the same transmission twice posts it once.

The webapp connects and hears nothing

  1. The proxy. A proxy that drops the upgrade headers answers the page and refuses the connection, and the page sits quiet. The four proxy lines in chapter 20 are the requirement.
  2. The access code. A server with an access list asks for a code, and a listener without one, or with one whose scope does not cover the talkgroup, sees nothing. Five attempts per session and per address, and the fifth is refused as locked out — a valid code included.
  3. The cap. MaxClients caps the connections the server takes, and a connection over the cap is refused in silence. The listeners count on the main screen is the number to look at before you look anywhere else.

The log is full of one message

Filter to the subsystem, read the counts strip, and read the message's own words: the messages this server writes name what happened and what it did about it. A message that repeats every hour is a scheduled pass failing, and a message that repeats on every call is a reference that does not resolve. Retention is the control that keeps the log the size you chose; the pass says what it removed, and says when it could not run.

The interface will not save

The save bar writes the working copy you have been editing. The conflict banner says another session saved that section while you were editing it: the server has one saved configuration, and it will not let a save overwrite what it has. Read the section as the server has it now, make your changes in it again, and save. Two people editing one section at the same time is the situation the banner is for, and the banner is the interface telling you before your work is written over, not after.

26 · Frequently asked questions

The questions an administrator asks, answered with the control that does the thing. Each answer points at the chapter that operates it.

How do I update from the version 5 program?

There is no upgrade from it: the version 6 server replaced the version 5 program, and what carries over is the database. Stop the old server, copy its database.sqlite into the new deployment's folder, rename the copy to rdio-scanner.db, and start the new program. On MySQL or MariaDB, back the database up and start the new program pointed at it with the -db_* flags. Chapter 24 is the path, with the migration it triggers and the archive that holds what cannot be carried.

I tried the automatic certificate and get strange errors

The authority verifies the name by reaching back to the machine it was asked for. The port the https listener answers on must be reachable from the internet, the domain must point at this machine, and the name you gave is the only name the server asks for. Chapter 19 is the certificate chapter, and its failure table is where the causes are listed.

The listener page keeps saying a new version is available

The page is a cached copy of the page the browser loaded before the update. Force a refresh (usually ctrl-shift-r), and if it keeps saying it, clear the site's stored data from the browser's site settings. It is the browser holding the old page, not the server holding a version notice.

How do I install ffmpeg on Windows?

You do not, for the deployment. Every release build carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio: the Windows amd64 build, the Linux builds for 386, ARM, ARM64 and amd64, and the macOS and FreeBSD builds, whose ffmpeg binaries this build compiles on those platforms with the one command go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg and adopts into the release. The container image is built from the linux-amd64 bundle. Install ffmpeg on the host only for a program you built yourself with plain go build, which carries none, and read the notice the server prints at startup, which is the program telling you which converter it found. Chapter 3 is the requirements chapter.

Which Mac do I build the macOS archives on?

Either one: the two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives. go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg there builds the ffmpeg of the machine it stands on, and go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 compiles the Intel binaries on that same Apple Silicon Mac, where Rosetta 2 is what lets the build run the binaries it compiled. An arm64 set compiled on an Intel Mac is run on an Apple Silicon Mac — the compile says so, and leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory for the other Mac. The target word is the one the release matrix spells, and the build also accepts the words go names a macOS machine by: darwin-amd64 is macos-amd64, and darwin-arm64 is macos-arm64. FreeBSD is the one target whose ffmpeg binaries are compiled only on FreeBSD. Chapter 21 is the chapter for each platform's service.

How do I put a reverse proxy in front of the server?

The proxy must carry the connection upgrade, because the listener's connection is a connection the browser opens through the same address as the page. HTTP/1.1, the Upgrade header, and a Connection header that follows the request: those are the requirement, and buffering and short timeouts are the two settings that break a deployment that otherwise works. Chapter 20 carries the nginx configuration, the Apache directives, and the trusted-proxy setting the proxy forces you to make.

How do I hear about a new release?

The project's repository watches its releases: the watch control on the repository tells you when a release is published, and the release is where the archive is. The release notes on the release, and the change log the repository publishes, are the release-by-release history; an archive carries the program, this guide, and the licence of the ffmpeg it embeds. Chapter 1 is the short list of what changed since the last published release.

How do I listen to several deployments from one browser?

Open each one with an id parameter that distinguishes it: http://localhost:3000/?id=dispatch. The talkgroup selections a listener makes are remembered per identifier; without it, every deployment shares one remembered selection, and the last one wins.

How do I change the access code a listener entered?

The code is stored in the browser's own storage. Append /reset to the address — http://localhost:3000/reset — and the page clears what it stored and returns to the main address. The code itself is issued, scoped, and expired in the Access section, chapter 9.

Where are the recordings stored?

In the database, in the call's own row. There is no recordings folder to keep in step with the database: the file that is the deployment is the file that holds the audio. Chapter 23 is the backup chapter, and it is short because of this.

Can I give a second person their own administrator login?

No. The deployment has one administrator credential, and it opens everything. The people who need to listen get access codes with a scope, an expiry, and a limit; the people who need to change the deployment share the administrator password, and the log is where you see what was changed. Chapter 22 is the credential model.

Why did my administrator sessions all end?

The signing secret changed. A start that made a secret, replaced one that was too short to be safe, or opened a database with a different secret ends every session signed with the old one, and says so on the console and in the log. Restoring a database is the same event. Chapter 22 is the credential chapter.

Can I move a deployment to another machine?

Install the program, copy the base directory, and start it. The ini file, the database with its recordings, and the autocert folder are the deployment. Expect the sessions to end, and expect the first start on a server database to apply the schema. Chapter 23 is the restore.

Does this guide cover the scanner webapp and the phone apps?

No. This guide is the server and its administration interface. The scanner webapp's own guide is the file docs/webapp.md in the repository, beside this one, and the native applications are the project's own apps. The webapp's behaviour is named here only where the server's settings change it — the access codes, the scope, the listener cap, the delay, and the alert tones are the server's decisions that the listener feels.

My question is not here

Ask it. The project takes questions on the repository's discussions, and the support address is in chapter 27. Before you ask, the log view is the deployment telling you what it saw, filtered by subsystem and by text, and it is the fastest way to turn a question into a report: what you expected, what the log says, and which subsystem said it.

The licence, and the two APIs

The software is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3: you may use it, modify it, and distribute it under those terms.

The HTTP REST API is not restricted. It is available under the GPL terms for every use, self-hosted deployments and third-party applications included: the endpoints in chapter 16 are yours to drive.

The WebSocket API — the connection a listener holds open, the one taken over the address the scanner webapp is served from — is a proprietary real-time channel provided by Saubeo Solutions, and it is the exception to the GPL position. It is available through Saubeo Solutions' hosted service for its native applications and the integrated scanner webapp. A self-hosted deployment answers the HTTP REST API without restriction; a self-hosted deployment whose own clients use the WebSocket API needs a prior written licence agreement with Saubeo Solutions. Authorized clients use the credentials Saubeo Solutions provides and do not share them.

The restrictions that go with that position: the WebSocket API is not used without authorization, not used in a commercial application or service without a licence agreement, not reverse-engineered, replicated, or redistributed, and not unlocked by modifying the code that restricts it. Access can be revoked, an agreement terminated, and unauthorized use pursued. The reason the project states is that the channel funds the development.

To ask about licensing, write to rdio-scanner@saubeo.solutions.

The ffmpeg licence

Every release build carries ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, and the archive carries FFMPEG.txt beside it: the licence terms of the components the build embeds, and what the binaries are. It says they are compiled for audio — no video codec, decoder, or encoder, and no network protocol is compiled into it — and for binaries the build adopted, it names the codecs the run recorded and the conversions it performed. For the Linux and Windows builds it names the source release, the digest, the configure recipe and the command that produced them, all reproducible from this project's own repository. For the macOS and FreeBSD builds it names the host that compiled them — this build, on a machine that runs the target's operating system, running the same trimmed build from the same source release the manifest pins, or binaries the project's maintainer compiled there and this build adopted — the command that built them there, and the codecs the run that adopted them asked them what they register. The run is the binaries' own execution, so the text names the host that ran them, and for binaries compiled across the two macOS architectures that is the other Mac: the Apple Silicon Mac that ran the Intel programs through Rosetta 2 is named as the host the release carries them from. A deployment that installs ffmpeg on the host — which a release deployment has no reason to do, and a program you built yourself with plain go build is the one case that needs it — takes the licence the package it installs carries.

Support

  • The log view, first. It is the deployment telling you what it saw, filtered by subsystem, by level, by date, and by text. A report that quotes it is answered faster than one that describes it.
  • The project's discussions, on the repository, are where questions and comments go, and where the answers become the documentation the next release carries.
  • rdio-scanner@saubeo.solutions is the address for support, and for the WebSocket API licence.
  • The project is funded by its sponsor and by sponsorship. A deployment that earns something from the project, or runs it for others, is the deployment the project asks to sponsor it. Starring the repository costs nothing and is appreciated.
